bodyText:
My daughter hit me in the face at the grocery store. In front of everyone.

She wanted something off the shelf but she couldn't tell me what it was. And I kept grabbing the wrong thing. 

So she hit me.

I put her in the cart and walked out without buying anything. 

I just sat in the car and cried.

My daughter was 2 years old, and she only had 6 words. 

And it had been like that for months.

Every day was the same thing. She'd want something, she couldn't tell me what it was, and the whole house would fall apart. 

Breakfast. Getting dressed. Bathtime. Bedtime. It didn't matter. 

Any moment where she needed something and couldn't say it turned into a war.

I tried everything people told me to try. 

I made routines. I gave warnings before transitions. I got down on her level and spoke calmly. I did time-outs. I did time-ins. I read every parenting article about managing toddler behavior.

None of it worked. 

And the more I paid attention, the more I realized the tantrums weren't about discipline at all.

Because they always started the same way. 

She'd want something. She'd try to tell me. I wouldn't understand. And then she'd lose it.

I could see it in her face right before the meltdown — she knew what she wanted to say, she just couldn't get it out. She was trapped. 

And the frustration had to go somewhere. So it came out through her body.

I knew that. Deep down I knew that. But I didn't know what to do about it.

So I tried working on her speech. I started narrating everything I did. I read to her every night. 

I bought flashcards and sat on the floor pointing at pictures saying "can you say dog?”

She'd stare at me. I'd wait. She'd stare. I'd try again. Nothing. And then she would start to cry. And then the crying would turn into a full meltdown. 

I would be sitting there on the floor with a stack of flashcards wondering how something that was supposed to help just made everything worse.

It kept happening. Every time I tried to practice with her it ended the same way. I'd put her on the spot, she'd freeze, the frustration would build, and she'd explode. 

The flashcards made her cry. Asking her to repeat words made her cry. Even pausing after I said something and waiting a few extra seconds to see if she'd try — stressed her out.

I was trying to help her talk. But everything I did felt like I was putting pressure on a kid who was already at her breaking point. 

I brought it up at her 2 year checkup.

I told the pediatrician about the meltdowns. How many we were having. How physical they were getting. How nothing I tried was helping.

She asked about routine and sleep and discipline. She said it could be behavioral. She said some kids just have bigger emotions at this age. 

She told me to stay consistent and gave me a handout on managing toddler behavior.

I sat in the parking lot staring at the handout. It was the same advice I'd been following for months. 

“Stay calm. Give warnings. Be consistent. Redirect.”

I'd been doing all of it. And my daughter was still hitting me in the face at grocery stores.

That night after we put her to sleep I started googling. "Why won't my toddler stop melting down." "2 year old tantrums getting worse." "Toddler aggressive when frustrated."

I read for hours. Most of it was the same behavioral advice all over again. Routines. Boundaries. Redirect.

But somewhere around midnight I found a video from a speech pathologist. She wasn't talking about behavior. 

She was talking about why toddlers with limited words have more meltdowns than other kids.

And the first thing she said stopped me.

She said if your child is having multiple meltdowns a day and has fewer than 20 words, it's probably not a behavior problem. It's a communication problem. 

And the worst thing you can do is put more pressure on them to speak.

She said every time we hold up an object and say "can you say this?" or pause and wait for them to fill in the word, the child feels it. 

They know we want something from them. And that pressure adds to the exact frustration that's already causing the meltdowns.

She said the answer isn't to practice more. It's to practice differently. 

She called it cause-and-effect play. Instead of the parent drilling words, the child drives it themselves. They press something, hear a word, and try to repeat it on their own terms. 

Without an adult standing over them. Just repetition at their own pace with zero pressure.

She said it's the number one method used in speech therapy clinics. And towards the end of the video she talked about a sound book that she helped design. 

The whole point of it was to take what works in the clinic and put it in the child's hands at home. 

Every page of the book has buttons they press to hear a word and repeat it back. 

And instead of the parent running the session, the child runs it. 

They press what they want. They hear it as many times as they want. If they feel like trying to say it, they try. If they don't, they don't. 

No one is watching. No one is waiting. 

She said that's why it works. Because the second you remove the audience, the kid stops freezing.

She said the kids who use it at home started saying words on their own within weeks. 

Not because anyone asked them to. Because they wanted to.

But I was still skeptical, because I know every kid is different, and I had already bought so many educational toys at that point. 

But it was $50. And this time the advice wasn't coming from another mom who "swore by it." 

It was coming from a speech pathologist who actually understood what my daughter was going through. 

So I ordered it.

The first week she pressed a few buttons and walked away. I didn't push it. I didn't sit next to her and try to turn it into a lesson. I just left it on the shelf where she could reach it.

By week two she started pulling it down on her own after breakfast. I'd hear it from the kitchen. 

The book would say a word and then I'd hear her voice a few seconds later trying to repeat it. Nothing clear yet. But she was trying. Her mouth was doing something it had never done before.

By week three the sounds were getting closer. She'd press the picture of the cat and the book would say "cat" and she'd say "cah." 

She'd press the dog and say "duh." 

She was playing the game mode over and over. 

The book would say "find the apple" and she'd press it and light up when she got it right.

No one was quizzing her. No one was hovering. Just her and the book.

About a month in I was washing dishes and she walked up and pulled on my leg. I looked down. She was holding her cup.

She looked at me and said "apple juice."

Not a scream. Not a cry. Not a meltdown. Just the word.

I handed it to her and turned around so she wouldn't see me crying. 

That was the first time in her life she had asked me for something with a word instead of a tantrum.

Two days later she pointed at her shoes and said "outside."

I didn't even hesitate. I put them on and we went. No guessing. No crying.

She told me what she wanted. And I gave it to her. And that was it.

After that, the meltdowns started disappearing. Not all at once. But the ones that came from not being able to communicate — the juice, the food, the shoes, the toys — those went away because she had the words now. 

She could say it instead of screaming it.

Our daycare lady pulled me aside at pickup and said her behavior had completely changed. 

She said my daughter was using words with the other kids, and she wasn't melting down in the classroom.

She said whatever we were doing at home to keep doing it.

2 weeks later, we went back for her 2 and a half year checkup. Same pediatrician. Same office.

The pediatrician started going through her usual checklist. She held up a picture of a dog to see if my daughter would point to it. 

My daughter looked at it and said "doggy."

The pediatrician looked at me over her glasses and said "well that's new."

She held up a few more. 

My daughter said "cat." 

Then she said "ball."

The pediatrician closed her chart. She said we didn't need the behavioral evaluation anymore.

She just wrote down the name of the sound book and nodded.

The book was designed by speech pathologists. It has 500 clearly spoken words.

Every page has a red start button and icons they can press to hear each word.

There are themed pages for feelings, food, animals, family, body parts, the house, the park, getting dressed. 

It has all the words they actually need to communicate. 

And each page has its own game that my daughter would play over and over.

The book says a word, she finds the matching picture, she presses it, and then tries to say it.  

She was practicing without it feeling like practice.

And she had free access to all of this whenever she wanted.

Which is the part I didn't understand until I watched that video. 

My daughter needed to be in control. She needed to decide when to press it, which word to hear, and how many times to hear it.

Because that’s when kids actually learn to talk. When they're the one driving it. Not when we're hovering with flashcards begging them to say a word.

There's also a phonics mode where the book teaches each letter's sound. So beyond learning words she's starting to piece together how they're built.

It's screen-free, and USB-C rechargeable so we're not fighting over dead batteries.

It's safety tested for little hands.

And the pages are thick and tear-proof so she can't rip them no matter how rough she plays with it. 

And unlike an iPad, when she's done with it she's calm. 

Not amped up. Not melting down.

It's the only thing that finally worked.

I'm not saying this is a miracle. I'm not saying it will work for every kid overnight because I was skeptical too.

But if your child is melting down every day and you've tried every behavioral strategy in the book and nothing is changing — it might not be a behavior problem. It might be a communication problem. 

And this book might be the thing that finally gives them the words they need so they don't have to scream for them anymore.

I found out yesterday they've been selling out constantly. If it's out of stock when you look, sign up for the restock alert. It usually comes back within a few days.

The link is below if you want to check it out. They are running a sale right now.

P.S. — I'm not a speech pathologist. I'm just a mom whose daughter went from 6 words and daily meltdowns to actually telling me what she needs. If your child has been evaluated and is in therapy, keep doing that. This isn't a replacement for professional help. It's the thing that finally made everything click at home when nothing else would.

P.P.S. — I keep getting asked what age this is good for. My daughter started using it at 2 and she's still using it now. I know friends whose kids started as young as 12 months. The book has enough in it that it grows with them. Worth the money either way.

My daughter said "mama" at 10 months and I cried. My son is 2 and I've never heard him say it.

I kept telling myself he would catch up.

It said "Between 20 and 30 percent of late talkers never fully catch up on their own. The first 36 months is when the brain is wiring itself for language. After that, the wiring slows down."

Every single thing I did with Emma.
 
None of it was working, and I finally understood why.

Kids don't build speech by hearing words. They build it by trying to say them.

Emma was a kid who did that on her own. 

From the moment she could sit up, she was babbling, repeating, trying sounds. 

Nothing I did built her speech — she was doing it herself.

He didn't need more listening. He needed practice trying to produce words on his own — without me hovering.

That's when learning actually sticks. When the kid is the one driving it.
 
There's also a phonics mode where the book teaches him how each letter sounds. 

So beyond learning words, he was starting to piece together how they were built.

It's safety tested for little hands.
 
And the pages are thick and tear-proof so he can't rip them no matter how rough he plays with it.
 
And unlike an iPad, when he's done with it he's calm. 

Not amped up. Not melting down.
 
It's the only thing that finally worked.

I've spent more time asking her to be quiet than most parents spend trying to get their kids to speak up.

And I'll admit — I was proud of that.
 
But then my son came along.
 
For the first year everything was fine. He hit every milestone Emma did. 

He sat up on time. Crawled on time. Walked at 12 months, just like her.
 
Then the words didn't come.
 
At 15 months he had 2 words. Emma had 15 by then.
 
At 18 months he had 3. Emma had over 30.
 
At 2 he only had 6.
 
I had been telling myself that “boys just talk later.”
 
Even though I had a 4-year-old at home who had been talking nonstop since she was 18 months old.
 
Even though I was Googling "how many words should a 2 year old have" at 1am almost every night.

I kept telling myself I was the only one worrying.

And then last month, Emma asked me a question I'd been afraid to ask myself.

We were at the park. She tugged on my sleeve and looked up at me. 

"Mommy, why doesn't Jack talk like other kids?"

I told her he was just a little behind and he'd catch up soon.

I don't think she believed me. Because a week later she asked me if he was ever going to talk to her.
 
That was the night I stopped pretending.
 
The next Monday I brought him to the pediatrician. It was a 12-minute appointment. 

She measured him. Weighed him. Listened to his heart. Then she asked if I had any concerns.
 
I told her he only had 6 words. That he understood everything I said but wouldn't speak. That my daughter was saying full sentences at his age.
 
She looked at his chart for maybe 4 seconds and said "boys just talk later than girls. Some are just late talkers. Come back at 2.5 if you're still worried."

I told her thank you and walked out. But something about that answer didn't sit right.

Because I already raised a kid who talked on time. 

I knew what it was supposed to look like.

And this wasn't it.
 
I couldn't sleep that night. I sat on the couch with my phone and started Googling again.
 
Somewhere around midnight I found a comment that stopped me cold.
 
It said "Between 20 and 30 percent of late talkers never fully catch up on their own. The first 36 months is when the brain is wiring itself for language. After that, the wiring slows down."
 
And my son only had 12 months left in that window.
 
I had been reading to him every night. Narrating my entire day out loud. Doing Ms. Rachel songs in the car. Buying flashcards. Signing up for a mommy-and-me class.
 
Every single thing I did with Emma.
 
None of it was working, and I finally understood why.

Kids don't build speech by hearing words. They build it by trying to say them.

Emma was a kid who did that on her own. 

From the moment she could sit up, she was babbling, repeating, trying sounds. 

Nothing I did built her speech — she was doing it herself.

Jack isn't wired that way. He needs a push to actually start trying. And nothing I'd been doing was giving him that.

Reading to him meant HE listened. Narrating meant HE listened. Ms. Rachel meant HE listened. 

Every single thing I'd been trying had him on the receiving end.

He didn't need more listening. He needed practice trying to produce words on his own — without me hovering.

That's what speech pathologists call cause-and-effect play. It's the #1 technique they use in-clinic. 

And I never gave him a chance to do it at home.
 
The next morning I called the pediatrician's office back and asked for a formal speech therapy referral. The waitlist for a private speech pathologist near me was 6 months.
 
I couldn't wait 6 months.
 
So I started doing more of my own research.
 
I joined 4 different Facebook groups for late talker parents. I followed every speech pathologist I could find on Instagram. I read Reddit threads until 1am looking for what actually worked for kids like mine.
 
Two days in, I saw a post that stopped me.
 
A mom whose son had been in the exact same spot as mine — understanding everything but not speaking — had found something that worked.
 
It was a sound book. Not a normal one — it was designed by speech pathologists specifically for how toddlers actually build language.
 
She said her son got obsessed with it right away. Every page had pictures he could press to hear the word out loud. 

There was also a game mode — the book would say a word, and he had to find the picture that matched.
 
She said he would sit with it for 30 minutes at a time saying the words along with the book. 

It was practice for him, but without any pressure.
 
And once the words felt easier to say, he started using them everywhere.
 
I sat there staring at the post for a while.
 
Because I'd read stories like this before. I'd already spent $180 on Lovevery flashcards that my son ignored after a week. 

Two months of Speech Blubs at $12/month that he barely touched. 

A stack of Melissa & Doug learning toys collecting dust in his closet.

Nothing had worked. I told myself every kid is different. What worked for her son might not work for mine. 

But it was $50. And I was desperate. So I ordered it.

He was thrilled every time he got it right. He'd play it over and over.
 
By week three I heard him. He was mumbling the words back to the book while he played. Not to me. To the book. But he was saying them.
 
By week four he was making sounds along with the book. Not real words yet. But attempts. Effort.
 
I felt something happening.
 
Then one morning I was making breakfast and Emma came running into the kitchen.
 
"Mom! Mom! He said my name!"
 
I turned around. My son was standing at the doorway holding the book.
 
He looked at Emma and said it again.
 
"Em-ma."
 
Two syllables. Clear as anything.
 
I sat down on the kitchen floor and cried into a dish towel.
 
Emma sat down next to me and held my hand and told me it was okay. 

She was 4 years old, patting me on the shoulder while I cried, and her brother was standing there saying her name.
 
Two weeks later he said "mama" for the first time.
 
Three weeks after that he asked for milk instead of screaming at the fridge.
 
After that he wouldn't stop. He was trying new words every single day. Some clear, some garbled, some just attempts. But he was doing it. 

He was talking.
 
And Emma started running the game mode with him. She'd sit on the floor and quiz him. 

She'd cheer every time he got one right. She was 4 years old and she'd become his speech coach.
 
Last week I took them both to the grocery store. He pointed at the fish tank and said "fish." 

A stranger overheard him and smiled at me.
 
It was the first time in 2 years I didn't feel embarrassed at the store.

Same pediatrician. Same office.

I stopped avoiding playdates. 

I stopped watching every other kid's mouth at the park to see how many words they had that mine didn't.
 
I stopped feeling like I had broken him.
 
I stopped feeling like I was failing at something I'd already done right once.
 
I got to just be his mom again. Not his monitor.
 
Last night Emma asked her brother what he wanted for a bedtime story. 

He walked over to the shelf, picked out a book, and handed it to her. He said "this one."
 
She looked at me and grinned like she'd won something.

She'd want something. She'd try to tell me. I wouldn't understand. And then she'd lose it.

I was trying to help her talk. But everything I did felt like I was putting pressure on a kid who was already at her breaking point.

I read for hours. Most of it was the same behavioral advice all over again. Routines. Boundaries. Redirect.

She was talking about why toddlers with limited words have more meltdowns than other kids.

My daughter hit me in the face at the grocery store. In front of everyone.

She wanted something off the shelf but she couldn't tell me what it was. And I kept grabbing the wrong thing. 

So she hit me.

I put her in the cart and walked out without buying anything. 

I just sat in the car and cried.

My daughter was 2 years old, and she only had 6 words. 

And it had been like that for months.

Every day was the same thing. She'd want something, she couldn't tell me what it was, and the whole house would fall apart. 

Breakfast. Getting dressed. Bathtime. Bedtime. It didn't matter. 

Any moment where she needed something and couldn't say it turned into a war.

I tried everything people told me to try. 

I made routines. I gave warnings before transitions. I got down on her level and spoke calmly. I did time-outs. I did time-ins. I read every parenting article about managing toddler behavior.

None of it worked. 

And the more I paid attention, the more I realized the tantrums weren't about discipline at all.

Because they always started the same way. 

She'd want something. She'd try to tell me. I wouldn't understand. And then she'd lose it.

I could see it in her face right before the meltdown — she knew what she wanted to say, she just couldn't get it out. She was trapped. 

And the frustration had to go somewhere. So it came out through her body.

I knew that. Deep down I knew that. But I didn't know what to do about it.

So I tried working on her speech. I started narrating everything I did. I read to her every night. 

I bought flashcards and sat on the floor pointing at pictures saying "can you say dog?”

She'd stare at me. I'd wait. She'd stare. I'd try again. Nothing. And then she would start to cry. And then the crying would turn into a full meltdown. 

I would be sitting there on the floor with a stack of flashcards wondering how something that was supposed to help just made everything worse.

It kept happening. Every time I tried to practice with her it ended the same way. I'd put her on the spot, she'd freeze, the frustration would build, and she'd explode. 

The flashcards made her cry. Asking her to repeat words made her cry. Even pausing after I said something and waiting a few extra seconds to see if she'd try — stressed her out.

I was trying to help her talk. But everything I did felt like I was putting pressure on a kid who was already at her breaking point. 

I brought it up at her 2 year checkup.

I told the pediatrician about the meltdowns. How many we were having. How physical they were getting. How nothing I tried was helping.

She asked about routine and sleep and discipline. She said it could be behavioral. She said some kids just have bigger emotions at this age. 

She told me to stay consistent and gave me a handout on managing toddler behavior.

I sat in the parking lot staring at the handout. It was the same advice I'd been following for months. 

“Stay calm. Give warnings. Be consistent. Redirect.”

I'd been doing all of it. And my daughter was still hitting me in the face at grocery stores.

That night after we put her to sleep I started googling. "Why won't my toddler stop melting down." "2 year old tantrums getting worse." "Toddler aggressive when frustrated."

I read for hours. Most of it was the same behavioral advice all over again. Routines. Boundaries. Redirect.

But somewhere around midnight I found a video from a speech pathologist. She wasn't talking about behavior. 

She was talking about why toddlers with limited words have more meltdowns than other kids.

And the first thing she said stopped me.

She said if your child is having multiple meltdowns a day and has fewer than 20 words, it's probably not a behavior problem. It's a communication problem. 

And the worst thing you can do is put more pressure on them to speak.

She said every time we hold up an object and say "can you say this?" or pause and wait for them to fill in the word, the child feels it. 

They know we want something from them. And that pressure adds to the exact frustration that's already causing the meltdowns.

She said the answer isn't to practice more. It's to practice differently. 

She called it cause-and-effect play. Instead of the parent drilling words, the child drives it themselves. They press something, hear a word, and try to repeat it on their own terms. 

Without an adult standing over them. Just repetition at their own pace with zero pressure.

She said it's the number one method used in speech therapy clinics. And towards the end of the video she talked about a sound book that she helped design. 

The whole point of it was to take what works in the clinic and put it in the child's hands at home. 

Every page of the book has buttons they press to hear a word and repeat it back. 

And instead of the parent running the session, the child runs it. 

They press what they want. They hear it as many times as they want. If they feel like trying to say it, they try. If they don't, they don't. 

No one is watching. No one is waiting. 

She said that's why it works. Because the second you remove the audience, the kid stops freezing.

She said the kids who use it at home started saying words on their own within weeks. 

Not because anyone asked them to. Because they wanted to.

But I was still skeptical, because I know every kid is different, and I had already bought so many educational toys at that point. 

But it was $50. And this time the advice wasn't coming from another mom who "swore by it." 

It was coming from a speech pathologist who actually understood what my daughter was going through. 

So I ordered it.

The first week she pressed a few buttons and walked away. I didn't push it. I didn't sit next to her and try to turn it into a lesson. I just left it on the shelf where she could reach it.

By week two she started pulling it down on her own after breakfast. I'd hear it from the kitchen. 

The book would say a word and then I'd hear her voice a few seconds later trying to repeat it. Nothing clear yet. But she was trying. Her mouth was doing something it had never done before.

By week three the sounds were getting closer. She'd press the picture of the cat and the book would say "cat" and she'd say "cah." 

She'd press the dog and say "duh." 

She was playing the game mode over and over. 

The book would say "find the apple" and she'd press it and light up when she got it right.

No one was quizzing her. No one was hovering. Just her and the book.

About a month in I was washing dishes and she walked up and pulled on my leg. I looked down. She was holding her cup.

She looked at me and said "apple juice."

Not a scream. Not a cry. Not a meltdown. Just the word.

I handed it to her and turned around so she wouldn't see me crying. 

That was the first time in her life she had asked me for something with a word instead of a tantrum.

Two days later she pointed at her shoes and said "outside."

I didn't even hesitate. I put them on and we went. No guessing. No crying.

She told me what she wanted. And I gave it to her. And that was it.

After that, the meltdowns started disappearing. Not all at once. But the ones that came from not being able to communicate — the juice, the food, the shoes, the toys — those went away because she had the words now. 

She could say it instead of screaming it.

Our daycare lady pulled me aside at pickup and said her behavior had completely changed. 

She said my daughter was using words with the other kids, and she wasn't melting down in the classroom.

She said whatever we were doing at home to keep doing it.

2 weeks later, we went back for her 2 and a half year checkup. Same pediatrician. Same office.

The pediatrician started going through her usual checklist. She held up a picture of a dog to see if my daughter would point to it. 

My daughter looked at it and said "doggy."

The pediatrician looked at me over her glasses and said "well that's new."

She held up a few more. 

My daughter said "cat." 

Then she said "ball."

The pediatrician closed her chart. She said we didn't need the behavioral evaluation anymore.

She just wrote down the name of the sound book and nodded.

The book was designed by speech pathologists. It has 500 clearly spoken words.

Every page has a red start button and icons they can press to hear each word.

There are themed pages for feelings, food, animals, family, body parts, the house, the park, getting dressed. 

It has all the words they actually need to communicate. 

And each page has its own game that my daughter would play over and over.

The book says a word, she finds the matching picture, she presses it, and then tries to say it.  

She was practicing without it feeling like practice.

And she had free access to all of this whenever she wanted.

Which is the part I didn't understand until I watched that video. 

My daughter needed to be in control. She needed to decide when to press it, which word to hear, and how many times to hear it.

Because that’s when kids actually learn to talk. When they're the one driving it. Not when we're hovering with flashcards begging them to say a word.

There's also a phonics mode where the book teaches each letter's sound. So beyond learning words she's starting to piece together how they're built.

It's screen-free, and USB-C rechargeable so we're not fighting over dead batteries.

It's safety tested for little hands.

And the pages are thick and tear-proof so she can't rip them no matter how rough she plays with it. 

And unlike an iPad, when she's done with it she's calm. 

Not amped up. Not melting down.

It's the only thing that finally worked.

I'm not saying this is a miracle. I'm not saying it will work for every kid overnight because I was skeptical too.

But if your child is melting down every day and you've tried every behavioral strategy in the book and nothing is changing — it might not be a behavior problem. It might be a communication problem. 

And this book might be the thing that finally gives them the words they need so they don't have to scream for them anymore.

The link is below if you want to check it out. They are running a sale right now.

P.S. — I'm not a speech pathologist. I'm just a mom whose daughter went from 6 words and daily meltdowns to actually telling me what she needs. If your child has been evaluated and is in therapy, keep doing that. This isn't a replacement for professional help. It's the thing that finally made everything click at home when nothing else would.

bodyText:
My daughter hit me in the face at the grocery store. In front of everyone.

She wanted something off the shelf but she couldn't tell me what it was. And I kept grabbing the wrong thing. 

So she hit me.

I put her in the cart and walked out without buying anything. 

I just sat in the car and cried.

My daughter was 2 years old, and she only had 6 words. 

And it had been like that for months.

Every day was the same thing. She'd want something, she couldn't tell me what it was, and the whole house would fall apart. 

Breakfast. Getting dressed. Bathtime. Bedtime. It didn't matter. 

Any moment where she needed something and couldn't say it turned into a war.

I tried everything people told me to try. 

I made routines. I gave warnings before transitions. I got down on her level and spoke calmly. I did time-outs. I did time-ins. I read every parenting article about managing toddler behavior.

None of it worked. 

And the more I paid attention, the more I realized the tantrums weren't about discipline at all.

Because they always started the same way. 

She'd want something. She'd try to tell me. I wouldn't understand. And then she'd lose it.

I could see it in her face right before the meltdown — she knew what she wanted to say, she just couldn't get it out. She was trapped. 

And the frustration had to go somewhere. So it came out through her body.

I knew that. Deep down I knew that. But I didn't know what to do about it.

So I tried working on her speech. I started narrating everything I did. I read to her every night. 

I bought flashcards and sat on the floor pointing at pictures saying "can you say dog?”

She'd stare at me. I'd wait. She'd stare. I'd try again. Nothing. And then she would start to cry. And then the crying would turn into a full meltdown. 

I would be sitting there on the floor with a stack of flashcards wondering how something that was supposed to help just made everything worse.

It kept happening. Every time I tried to practice with her it ended the same way. I'd put her on the spot, she'd freeze, the frustration would build, and she'd explode. 

The flashcards made her cry. Asking her to repeat words made her cry. Even pausing after I said something and waiting a few extra seconds to see if she'd try — stressed her out.

I was trying to help her talk. But everything I did felt like I was putting pressure on a kid who was already at her breaking point. 

I brought it up at her 2 year checkup.

I told the pediatrician about the meltdowns. How many we were having. How physical they were getting. How nothing I tried was helping.

She asked about routine and sleep and discipline. She said it could be behavioral. She said some kids just have bigger emotions at this age. 

She told me to stay consistent and gave me a handout on managing toddler behavior.

I sat in the parking lot staring at the handout. It was the same advice I'd been following for months. 

“Stay calm. Give warnings. Be consistent. Redirect.”

I'd been doing all of it. And my daughter was still hitting me in the face at grocery stores.

That night after we put her to sleep I started googling. "Why won't my toddler stop melting down." "2 year old tantrums getting worse." "Toddler aggressive when frustrated."

I read for hours. Most of it was the same behavioral advice all over again. Routines. Boundaries. Redirect.

But somewhere around midnight I found a video from a speech pathologist. She wasn't talking about behavior. 

She was talking about why toddlers with limited words have more meltdowns than other kids.

And the first thing she said stopped me.

She said if your child is having multiple meltdowns a day and has fewer than 20 words, it's probably not a behavior problem. It's a communication problem. 

And the worst thing you can do is put more pressure on them to speak.

She said every time we hold up an object and say "can you say this?" or pause and wait for them to fill in the word, the child feels it. 

They know we want something from them. And that pressure adds to the exact frustration that's already causing the meltdowns.

She said the answer isn't to practice more. It's to practice differently. 

She called it cause-and-effect play. Instead of the parent drilling words, the child drives it themselves. They press something, hear a word, and try to repeat it on their own terms. 

Without an adult standing over them. Just repetition at their own pace with zero pressure.

She said it's the number one method used in speech therapy clinics. And towards the end of the video she talked about a sound book that she helped design. 

The whole point of it was to take what works in the clinic and put it in the child's hands at home. 

Every page of the book has buttons they press to hear a word and repeat it back. 

And instead of the parent running the session, the child runs it. 

They press what they want. They hear it as many times as they want. If they feel like trying to say it, they try. If they don't, they don't. 

No one is watching. No one is waiting. 

She said that's why it works. Because the second you remove the audience, the kid stops freezing.

She said the kids who use it at home started saying words on their own within weeks. 

Not because anyone asked them to. Because they wanted to.

But I was still skeptical, because I know every kid is different, and I had already bought so many educational toys at that point. 

But it was $50. And this time the advice wasn't coming from another mom who "swore by it." 

It was coming from a speech pathologist who actually understood what my daughter was going through. 

So I ordered it.

The first week she pressed a few buttons and walked away. I didn't push it. I didn't sit next to her and try to turn it into a lesson. I just left it on the shelf where she could reach it.

By week two she started pulling it down on her own after breakfast. I'd hear it from the kitchen. 

The book would say a word and then I'd hear her voice a few seconds later trying to repeat it. Nothing clear yet. But she was trying. Her mouth was doing something it had never done before.

By week three the sounds were getting closer. She'd press the picture of the cat and the book would say "cat" and she'd say "cah." 

She'd press the dog and say "duh." 

She was playing the game mode over and over. 

The book would say "find the apple" and she'd press it and light up when she got it right.

No one was quizzing her. No one was hovering. Just her and the book.

About a month in I was washing dishes and she walked up and pulled on my leg. I looked down. She was holding her cup.

She looked at me and said "apple juice."

Not a scream. Not a cry. Not a meltdown. Just the word.

I handed it to her and turned around so she wouldn't see me crying. 

That was the first time in her life she had asked me for something with a word instead of a tantrum.

Two days later she pointed at her shoes and said "outside."

I didn't even hesitate. I put them on and we went. No guessing. No crying.

She told me what she wanted. And I gave it to her. And that was it.

After that, the meltdowns started disappearing. Not all at once. But the ones that came from not being able to communicate — the juice, the food, the shoes, the toys — those went away because she had the words now. 

She could say it instead of screaming it.

Our daycare lady pulled me aside at pickup and said her behavior had completely changed. 

She said my daughter was using words with the other kids, and she wasn't melting down in the classroom.

She said whatever we were doing at home to keep doing it.

2 weeks later, we went back for her 2 and a half year checkup. Same pediatrician. Same office.

The pediatrician started going through her usual checklist. She held up a picture of a dog to see if my daughter would point to it. 

My daughter looked at it and said "doggy."

The pediatrician looked at me over her glasses and said "well that's new."

She held up a few more. 

My daughter said "cat." 

Then she said "ball."

The pediatrician closed her chart. She said we didn't need the behavioral evaluation anymore.

She just wrote down the name of the sound book and nodded.

The book was designed by speech pathologists. It has 500 clearly spoken words.

Every page has a red start button and icons they can press to hear each word.

There are themed pages for feelings, food, animals, family, body parts, the house, the park, getting dressed. 

It has all the words they actually need to communicate. 

And each page has its own game that my daughter would play over and over.

The book says a word, she finds the matching picture, she presses it, and then tries to say it.  

She was practicing without it feeling like practice.

And she had free access to all of this whenever she wanted.

Which is the part I didn't understand until I watched that video. 

My daughter needed to be in control. She needed to decide when to press it, which word to hear, and how many times to hear it.

Because that’s when kids actually learn to talk. When they're the one driving it. Not when we're hovering with flashcards begging them to say a word.

There's also a phonics mode where the book teaches each letter's sound. So beyond learning words she's starting to piece together how they're built.

It's screen-free, and USB-C rechargeable so we're not fighting over dead batteries.

It's safety tested for little hands.

And the pages are thick and tear-proof so she can't rip them no matter how rough she plays with it. 

And unlike an iPad, when she's done with it she's calm. 

Not amped up. Not melting down.

It's the only thing that finally worked.

I'm not saying this is a miracle. I'm not saying it will work for every kid overnight because I was skeptical too.

But if your child is melting down every day and you've tried every behavioral strategy in the book and nothing is changing — it might not be a behavior problem. It might be a communication problem. 

And this book might be the thing that finally gives them the words they need so they don't have to scream for them anymore.

I found out yesterday they've been selling out constantly. If it's out of stock when you look, sign up for the restock alert. It usually comes back within a few days.

The link is below if you want to check it out. They are running a sale right now.

P.S. — I'm not a speech pathologist. I'm just a mom whose daughter went from 6 words and daily meltdowns to actually telling me what she needs. If your child has been evaluated and is in therapy, keep doing that. This isn't a replacement for professional help. It's the thing that finally made everything click at home when nothing else would.

P.P.S. — I keep getting asked what age this is good for. My daughter started using it at 2 and she's still using it now. I know friends whose kids started as young as 12 months. The book has enough in it that it grows with them. Worth the money either way.

bodyText:
200 words. That's the average for a 2-year-old. My son had 6.

I had been telling myself he was fine for months.

The kind of "fine" where I kept adding one more thing to our bedtime routine, praying something would click.

Reading a little longer at bedtime. Adding another Ms. Rachel song to the car ride. Buying another set of flashcards.

Convincing myself each new thing would be the one that clicked.

Nothing clicked.

Then we went to my niece's 2nd birthday party. That was the day it hit me.

She's 4 months younger than my son. 

She spent the whole party running up to her mom saying "cake please", "more juice", "look mama look." 

Full little sentences.

Meanwhile my son sat on my lap the whole time, pointing at things and grunting.

When we were leaving, my niece followed us to the driveway to wave goodbye. She said "bye Auntie" clear as day.

My son was on my hip. Silent.

The next Monday I called our pediatrician's office and asked for the first available appointment. 

They squeezed us in on Thursday.
 
The appointment lasted 12 minutes total. 

She measured him. Weighed him. Listened to his heart. Then asked if I had any concerns.
 
I told her he only had 6 words. That he understood everything I said but wouldn't speak. That every kid I knew his age was stringing sentences together and mine was still pointing.
 
She looked at his chart for maybe 4 seconds and said "he's within range for boys. Some are just late talkers. Come back at 2.5 if you're still worried."
 
I sat in the parking lot afterward for 20 minutes trying to figure out why I felt worse than when I walked in.
 
Because I knew. I already knew.
 
The signs had been there for months and I'd been finding a reason to ignore every one of them.
 
He stopped babbling around 14 months. I told myself he was just quiet.
 
He'd grunt and point instead of trying to say what he wanted. I told myself he was just efficient.
 
He shut down every time I asked him to say a word. I told myself he was just stubborn.
 
At his 18-month checkup he had 3 words. I told myself the pediatrician said boys just talk later.
 
At his 2-year checkup he had 6. I told myself at least it was more than 3.
 
Every red flag, I painted white.
 
That night I couldn't sleep. I sat on the couch with my phone and started Googling.
 
Somewhere around midnight I found a comment that stopped me cold.
 
"Between 20 and 30 percent of late talkers never fully catch up on their own. And the first 36 months of a kid's life is when the brain is wiring itself for language. After age 3, the wiring slows down."
 
My son had 12 months left in that window.
 
I sat there and stared at the wall for probably 20 minutes.
 
Because everything I'd been doing suddenly made sense in a way I didn't want it to.
 
I'd read to him every single night since he was born. Narrated my entire day out loud like a lunatic. Cut screens. Did Ms. Rachel songs in the car. Signed up for early intervention. 

Bought $200 worth of flashcards from Lovevery. Subscribed to Speech Blubs. Put him in daycare so he'd be around other kids.
 
None of it had worked.
 
And I finally understood why.
 
Kids don't build speech by hearing words. They build it by actually trying to say them.
 
Every single thing I'd been doing — my son was on the receiving end. He was passive. 

He was listening but he was never DOING.
 
It's the difference between watching someone ride a bike and being put on one. You can watch a bike your whole life and never learn to ride it.
 
Speech pathologists call it cause-and-effect play. It's the #1 technique they use in-clinic. 

And it works because the kid is the one driving it — pressing, hearing, and trying to repeat, hundreds of times a day, without any pressure or adult hovering.
 
I sat there at 1am and realized I'd been trying to teach my son to talk by talking AT him for 2 years.
 
The next morning I called the pediatrician back and asked for a formal speech therapy referral. 

The waitlist for a private speech pathologist near me was 6 months.
 
I couldn't wait 6 months.

So I started doing my own research. 

I joined 4 different Facebook groups for late talker parents. I followed every speech pathologist I could find on Instagram. I read Reddit threads until 1am looking for what actually worked for kids like mine.
 
Two days in, I saw a post that stopped me.

A mom whose son had been in the exact same spot as mine — understanding everything but not speaking — had found something that worked. 

It was a sound book — designed by speech pathologists.

She said her son got obsessed with it right away. 

Every page had pictures he could press to hear the word out loud. There was also a game mode where the book would say a word, and he had to find the picture that matched.

He'd sit with it for 30 minutes at a time saying the words along with the book. 

It was practice for him, but without any pressure.
 
And once the words felt easier to say, he started using them everywhere.

It sounded almost too good. And that was the problem.
 
Because I'd been down this road before. 

I'd already spent $180 on Lovevery flashcards that my son ignored after a week.
 
Two months of Speech Blubs at $12/month that he barely touched. 

A stack of Melissa & Doug learning toys collecting dust in his closet.

Nothing had worked.

And I know every kid is different, so what worked for her son might not work for mine.

But it was $50. And I was desperate. So I ordered it.
 
The first week I didn't see much. He held it, pressed some buttons, wandered off. I remember thinking great, another $50 down the drain.
 
But by week two, he'd started sitting with it every morning after breakfast. On his own. I didn't put it in front of him. 

He'd get up, pull it off the shelf, and sit on the rug flipping pages.
 
The game mode was what really got him. The book would call out "find the elephant" and he'd have to press the elephant. He was thrilled every time he got it right. He'd play it over and over.
 
By week three I heard him. He was mumbling the words back to the book while he played. Not to me. To the book. But he was saying them.
 
By week four he was making sounds along with the book. Not real words yet. But attempts. Effort.
 
Something was happening.
 
About a month in, I was making dinner and he walked up to me at the counter and said "up." With his arms out.
 
He wanted to be picked up.
 
He'd never once asked me for anything with a word. He'd always grab my leg and whine. 

I put down the spatula, picked him up, and cried into his hair.
 
Because in 2 years, that had never happened.
 
Not once.
 
Two weeks later he said his cousin's name for the first time. 

Three weeks after that he asked for milk instead of screaming at the fridge.
 
After that he wouldn't stop. He was trying new words every single day. Some clear, some garbled, some just attempts. But he was doing it. He was talking.
 
Last week I took him to the grocery store. He pointed at the fish tank and said "fish." 

A stranger overheard him and smiled at me.
 
First time in 2 years I didn't feel embarrassed at the store.
 
We went back for his 2.5 year checkup last month.
 
Same pediatrician. Same office.
 
He'd gone from 6 words to over 50.
 
She looked at his chart from 6 months ago and then looked at me. She said "I don't even know what to write here."

She told me I could go ahead and cancel the speech therapy referral — he wouldn't need it anymore.
 
She wrote down the name of the sound book and nodded.
 
And here's the part I didn't expect.
 
I got myself back too.
 
I stopped Googling "how many words should a 2-year-old have" at 2am every night. 

I stopped avoiding the family group chat. I stopped dreading playdates. 

I stopped watching every other kid's mouth at the park to see how many words they had that mine didn't.
 
I got to just be his mom again. Not his monitor.
 
The book was designed by speech pathologists. It has 500 clearly spoken words in it.
 
Every page has a red start button and icons he could press to hear each word.
 
There were themed pages for the zoo, the doctor's office, construction, the solar system, feelings, opposites — 23 themed worlds in total.
 
And each page had its own little game he'd play over and over.
 
My son had free access to any of them, whenever he wanted, just by pressing a button.
 
Which is the part I didn’t realize was so important.
 
He was in control. He decided when to press it, which word to hear, and how many times to hear it.
 
That's when learning actually sticks. When the kid is the one driving it.
 
There's also a phonics mode where the book teaches him each letter's sound. 

So beyond learning words, he was starting to piece together how they were built.
 
It's screen-free, and USB-C rechargeable so we're not fighting over dead batteries.
 
And it's safety tested for little hands.
 
The pages are thick and tear-proof so he can't rip them no matter how rough he plays with it.
 
And unlike an iPad, when he's done with it he's calm. Not amped up. Not melting down.
 
It's the only thing that finally worked.
 
I'm not saying it's a miracle. I'm not saying it will work for every kid overnight.
 
But I am saying if your kid is where mine was — understanding everything and just not able to get the words out — this is worth trying while there's still time in the window that matters.
 
I found out yesterday they've been selling out constantly. If it's out of stock when you look, sign up for the restock alert. It usually comes back within a few days.
 
The link is below if you want to check it out. They are running a back to school sale right now.
 
P.S. — I'm not a speech pathologist. I'm just a mom who found something that worked for us after 2 years of trying everything else. If your child has been evaluated and is in therapy, keep doing that. This isn't a replacement for professional help. It's the thing that made all the other stuff we were doing actually stick.

bodyText:
This is my back seat after three hours on the highway with two kids.

A 4 year old and a 1 year old. I took the photo in the driveway before I cleaned anything, so I'd remember it next time I packed.

Crayons ground into the seat. A pouch squeezed flat. Stickers on the window. One shoe. I still don't know where the other one went.

Every single thing in that back seat bought me about ten minutes.

The crayons lasted until the first one rolled under the seat. Then everyone cried, because nobody can reach the crayon under the seat at 65 on the highway.

The stickers went on the window and stayed there. The snack pouch bought us one exit. The little car got thrown at his sister, because when the older one runs out of things to do, he goes for her.

And yes, at one point the phone went back over my shoulder. Anyone who has had a screaming toddler and a screaming baby in the same car has done it. I'm not sorry.

But sitting there in the driveway, I kept wondering why a whole bag of toys ran out before the halfway mark.

Was it the drive? The kids? Or was I packing the wrong kind of thing entirely?

A childcare educator who has done this drive more times than she'd like to count wrote down the six toys that actually last in a car. Her answer to that question surprised me, and it wasn't "pack more."

My name is Tania, and I’m a mom from Boston and the founder of the award-winning Go Go Singing Sound Book series.
When my son was a baby, I wanted him to grow up surrounded by music and faith — to feel God’s stories, not just hear them. But every Christian sound book I found had tinny music, fake kid sounds, or flat, low-quality art. None told the full stories of the Bible.
So, I decided to make my own — for him, and for other children too. Sound books that bring the Bible to life and make kids sing and dance. 🎶
Inspired by my experience learning three languages and three instruments, I teamed up with musicians and singers around the world to create fun, multicultural music that shows God's love for people all around the world. 🌍✝️
In just two years, we produced over 200 songs — from Sunday school classics to original Bible-based tunes. We tested hundreds of versions, perfected our audio chips, and even visited factories to make sure every sound book met our standards.
After months of recording, revising, and testing songs with real families, we created something truly special:
 Six Bible sound books with 58 joyful songs that kids love to sing and dance to — featuring real instruments and real parent-and-child voices on premium speakers.
Even my toddler son and his grandma helped us test them. If they didn’t love a song instantly, we’d fix it until they did. 💛
Within a few months of launching, we sold over 12,000 books.
This isn’t just a book — it’s a fun, musical way to share God’s Word with your little ones.
I’ve loved creating them, and I hope you love them as much as we do. 💖

 Six Bible sound books with 58 joyful songs that kids love to sing and dance to — featuring real instruments and real parent-and-child voices on premium speakers.

Within a few months of launching, we sold over 12,000 books.
This isn’t just a book — it’s a fun, musical way to share God’s Word with your little ones.

bodyText:
I bought this before she was born, and I'm a bit embarrassed it's still in the box.

That's the rainbow stacker on the top shelf of her room.
You can see the dust on the box if you zoom in.

I'd seen it in so many of those calm playroom videos.
I pictured her on a rug with it, in soft afternoon light.

Under it, three puzzles, still in the plastic.

I kept saying she wasn't ready yet.
The truth is I didn't know how to get her started.
So it went up high, out of the way, and I kept buying other things.

It's out of the box now. I'll get to why.

I should say up front, I'm the mom who saves toy rotation reels.

The calm shelves, four things out at a time. I have a whole folder of them.

Our real toy room looks nothing like that. It's plastic, most of it lights up, and a lot of it plays the same song when you step on it in the dark.

Some of it was gifts. A lot of it was me, in a toy aisle at 6pm, thinking this might finally be the one she plays with.

Rosie would press a button, watch it flash, and walk straight back out to find me.

I added it up once in my notes app. Every toy in that room. Then I deleted the note before my husband could see it.

The rainbow stacker I wanted before she was born is still in its box on the top shelf. I kept telling myself she wasn't ready for it.

Then she turned two.

Both sets of grandparents. Two aunties. Half of daycare. By Sunday night the toy room floor was new boxes and torn paper.

On the Monday morning the house went quiet. The kind of quiet that makes you put your coffee down.

I found her in the kitchen. She'd pulled out the bottom drawer, the one with all the container lids, and she was sitting in front of it with her legs stuck straight out. Pushing a lid onto a container. Pulling it off. Trying another one.

Forty minutes. I checked the oven clock twice. She hummed the whole time.

I laughed out loud, alone in my kitchen. Then I looked down the hall at a room full of birthday presents and felt so stupid about the money my face went hot.

That night at 11:40pm I was in bed typing "toddler won't play with toys". Then "why does my toddler get bored of toys so fast".

It was all stuff I'd already tried:

🧺 Toy rotation. A whole afternoon setting up the shelf. It lasted nine days.

💡 The light-up learning toys. She'd watch one for about a minute, like a tiny show, then wander off.

🧩 The "open-ended" toys everyone recommends. I just didn't know how to get her started, and she could tell.

📦 A monthly toy subscription box. Half of every box stayed in the box.

Every fix was me buying another thing. None of it started with what she was actually doing.

So I tried the one idea that was free. For a week I wrote down what she kept going back to.

Here's the list, straight off my phone:
👜 The zip on my handbag
🚪 The latch on the side gate
🥣 The lid of the container
🚗 The buckle on her car seat, which she now insists on doing herself

I spent more of my best friend's visit under this table than at it.

This is the café floor, taken from my knees.
A squashed bit of banana.
A crayon, the third one to go over the edge.
The teaspoon, which I'd picked up twice already.
And the wheel of the stroller she climbed in and out of the whole time.
My best friend had flown in for one day to see me.
Every time I came back up, I'd lost the thread of what she was saying.
I don't think she ever got to finish a story either.

Jess has been my best friend since we were fourteen. She lives a flight away now, and two months ago she flew in for one day, just to see me.

We met at the café near my house at 10am. Me, Jess, and Mila, who is two.

We were there for 90 minutes. I did not finish one sentence.

Not one. Every time I got halfway, Mila needed something. Down from the chair. Back up. The sugar sachets. My spoon. My face, turned towards her with both her hands.

Jess was lovely about it. She'd start telling me about her new job and I'd say "sorry, keep going" and she'd say "no, it's fine," and neither of us ever found where she'd stopped.

My latte went cold with the heart still on top.

At the door I hugged her and said "sorry, next time properly."

She said "of course, love you."

It was the kindest thing she could have said. That's why I cried at the first red light.

On the drive home I worked it out. I hadn't finished a conversation with another adult in two years. Not with anyone.

And the invitations had quietly stopped. Nobody fell out with me. The group chat just started making plans I found out about afterwards, from photos.

I didn't blame them. For two years I'd been the friend who says "next time properly."

That night I was in bed by 8:30 with my phone, typing "toddler interrupts every conversation" and then "how to have a coffee with a toddler".

Every answer said to teach her to wait her turn. She's two.

And I'd already tried everything I could think of:

🌳 The park instead of a café. Mila runs, I chase, my friend stands by the swings holding both coffees. We talk in twelve-second pieces.

📱 My phone propped against the sugar jar. Twenty quiet minutes, with me half-listening over a cartoon. I still do this in the car sometimes. Screens aren't the enemy. But I wasn't really at that table either.

🌙 Meeting after her bedtime. I'm asleep by 9. I tried twice and yawned through the second one.

🥛 Babycinos. Gone in two minutes. Then she wants mine.

Every fix bought me a few minutes. None of them bought me a conversation.

At 8:52 Jess texted. She's been a nanny for ten years, and I'd honestly forgotten, because to me she's just Jess.

"She's not being difficult. She's two, there's nothing for her hands, and we were doing the one thing she can't join."

I read it about six times.

Talking was the one thing at that table Mila couldn't be part of. Jess and I each had a cup to hold while we talked. Mila had nothing.

Of course she climbed into the middle of it. It was the only way in.

She wasn't interrupting us. She was trying to join.

Jess sent one more message. Give her something of her own to work on, right next to your cup. Lots of steps. Silent. She's busy with her thing while you do yours.

I thought it sounded nice and wouldn't last five minutes in a café. Mila gets bored of new toys before I've got the packaging in the bin.

Then Jess sent a photo of the one she takes to work. A soft felt busy board that zips shut like a book. Buckles, a zip, laces, snaps, little velcro pieces. No sound. The pages come off, so you can hand over one at a time.

I ordered one before I put my phone down.

The first test was a Thursday, with Claire, a friend from my old work I hadn't seen in over a year. I texted her "coffee? warning, Mila's coming."

Our drinks came. I unzipped the board and put one page next to my cup. The buckle page.

Mila clicked it shut. Opened it. Clicked it shut. Then the zip, then the laces, frowning at it like it was very important work.

Claire told me about her sister's wedding. The whole thing, start to finish.

I heard the ending.

Then I told her something, and I finished it. Then I drank my latte, and it was still warm, and I nearly cried into it.

That was seven Thursdays ago. It's our standing coffee now. We share a slice of cake. Mila asks for "my work" when she sees me pick up my keys.

Jess is coming back next month. For the first time in two years, I'm not dreading the goodbye.

I don't think friends stop inviting you because they stop loving you. I think they stop because every visit ends with "next time properly."

Next time properly turned out to be a Thursday.

I heard the fridge door open from the couch and I didn't move. I couldn't.

The baby was halfway through a feed.
I called out her name. Then again.
I heard the stool scrape across the floor.
Then the fridge started beeping because the door had been open too long.
By the time he finished and I got there, it looked like this.
The yogurt tipped over on the bottom shelf.
Her little stool pushed right up to the door.
His bottle still on the counter where I'd left it.
I stood there with a baby on my shoulder and just looked at it.
This was most days.

When Max was born, Evie was two and a half.

He feeds about eight times a day, 40 minutes each. For the first two weeks she kissed his head every morning like he was a present someone had left for her.

Then she worked out what a feed means.

It means mommy sits down and can't get up.

So every feed, she found something. She climbed the back of the couch. She opened the fridge and stood in it. She drew on the hallway wall, low down, right where I could see it and couldn't reach it. She pulled every tissue out of the box, one at a time, looking at me the whole way.

Eight times a day. I started to dread the little snuffling noises Max makes when he's hungry, because I knew what came next.

Everyone said she's jealous, it's normal, you ride it out. So I rode it out, and tried everything else too:

🧺 The special feeding-time basket, with books and toys that only came out for feeds. Tipped onto the rug in about three minutes, and she was back on the couch arm.

👶 "Involve her." She fetched me a nappy once, so proud of herself, and that job lasted one minute. That left 39 minutes of the feed.

🍎 A snack at every feed. She ate it. Then she wouldn't touch her dinner.

📺 The TV at every feed. It worked, I won't pretend it didn't. But eight feeds a day is a lot of TV, and I could feel it adding up in both of us.

Then one afternoon in week four, I was pinned in the corner of the couch halfway through a feed, and it went quiet. I leaned over as far as I could without unlatching him. The nappy cream. The whole tube, smeared into the cushions in big white handprints.

I didn't yell. I just cried. Sat there with the baby still feeding and cried where she could see me.

And she came over, climbed up next to me, put her face right up close to mine and said, "Mommy sad?"

That undid me. She wasn't trying to be bad. She was right there, worried about me, and I'd spent weeks thinking of her as the problem.

That night at 2:10am, feeding again, I typed "toddler acting out while I feed the baby" and then "toddler jealous of newborn". Every answer said extra attention, one-on-one time, be patient.

I was never alone with her. That was the whole problem.

At the six-week home visit, the child health nurse sat on our ottoman with her notes while I fed Max. Evie did her whole routine. Up the couch. Down. Tissue box. Fridge door.

The nurse watched the entire feed and didn't write a thing. Then she said, "She's not jealous of the baby. She's jealous of your hands."

I laughed. Then I couldn't stop thinking about it.

For 40 minutes, my hands are full and hers are empty. Every other part of the day I'm her climbing frame, her helper, her toy. The feed is the one time I can't be. So her hands go looking for something, and what's in reach is the fridge and the wall.

Nothing I'd tried lasted as long as a feed.

She needed a job that was only hers, right next to me, with enough steps to outlast her brother.

I figured that works on other people's kids. I ordered a pink felt busy board anyway. A soft one that zips shut like a book, with buckles, zips, laces and snaps across the pages.

One rule. It comes out when the feeding pillow comes out, and goes away when the pillow does. It's not an anytime toy. It's her feed job.

The first feed, she did the buckle page, then undid every lace, then asked me to do them back up so she could undo them again. Max finished. I looked at the clock. She hadn't left the couch once.

That was three weeks ago.

Now when Max makes his hungry noises, Evie says "baby's hungry" and goes to get her board. She sits against my arm and works through the pages while he feeds. Sometimes she tells him about it. "Max. Buckle. Click."

I get to look at both of them. I drink my water while it's still cold. Some feeds I actually close my eyes.

The TV still goes on some afternoons when I'm wrecked. It's just not eight times a day anymore, and I'm not crying on the couch.

If you're feeding a newborn while your toddler climbs the walls: she isn't being naughty, and you're not doing it wrong. Her hands just have nothing to do at the one time yours can't help.

Confession: I took this photo instead of opening the door.

I was kneeling on the bath mat in a towel, hair still full of shampoo.

Those are his fingers under the door. Four of them, wiggling at me from the hallway.

He'd been calling me for about three minutes. It felt like thirty.

And instead of opening the door, I took a photo.

I think I needed someone, anyone, to see what my mornings looked like. Dan was already at work. There was nobody else to show.

I opened it ten seconds later and rinsed the shampoo out with him hugging my wet leg.

That's how it went, every day, for a long time.

My son Theo is two. For seven months, I did not shower alone once.

My partner Dan leaves for work at 5:30, so mornings are just us. The second the bathroom door clicks shut, Theo is on the other side.

First the knocking. Then "Mama? Mama?" Then four little fingers under the door, checking I'm still in there.

Then the crying.

I got fast. Shampoo in, shampoo out. Conditioner went in and stayed in, because rinsing it meant another minute of him sobbing at the door.

I told myself it was a phase. Just who he is. Some kids are cuddly. Mine was velcro.

Then one Thursday I turned the shower on, wrapped myself in a towel and sat down on the closed toilet lid.

I left the water running so he'd think I was busy.

I just wanted two minutes where nobody was touching me. So I sat there in a towel, hiding from my own son, listening to him cry through the door.

I hated myself for it.

That night at 11:40 I was in bed typing "toddler won't let me leave the room" into my phone. Then "2 year old follows me everywhere".

I'd already tried most of what came up:

🚧 A playpen outside the bathroom door. He stood at the bars and screamed my name instead.

🧺 A special bathroom toy basket. Two good mornings, then he was back at the door.

🚿 Bringing him in the shower with me. I spent the whole time stopping him slipping on the tiles. Very clean toddler. Still unwashed mom.

📺 The TV on in the next room. Four minutes, then he came looking for me.

😢 "Just let him cry, he'll learn." He didn't. I did. I learned to wash my hair faster.

Every one of them moved the crying somewhere else. None of them stopped it.

Then one Tuesday, he went quiet.

Twelve minutes of quiet outside the door. With a two year old that's scarier than crying, so I got out dripping and opened it.

He'd found my makeup bag. He was sitting on the carpet zipping it open and shut. Open, shut, open, shut. Lids off my lipsticks and back on. A mascara, a hair clip and a tiny mirror lined up in a row, then all over again.

He didn't even look up at me.

I stood there in my towel and it finally made sense.

It was never about me leaving. Everything in our house is exactly where it was yesterday. His toys do the same thing every time. Then there's me. Water running, drawers opening, things going on and coming off. I'm the only thing in the house that keeps changing.

So he follows me. Little hands with nothing new go looking for the one thing that changes.

That makeup bag had a next thing. A zip, then a lid, then a row to make. Every time he finished something, something else was waiting.

So I stopped trying to get him away from the door, and started putting something with a next step right where he lands.

I didn't think a toy stood a chance. He'd walked past every toy we own to sit against that door.

But I found a soft felt busy board that folds shut like a book. Every page is a different job. A buckle, then a zip, then laces, then shapes to match.

I put a spare bath mat in the hallway, right where he always sits, and opened the board on it.

First morning, I heard his fingers under the door once. Then a click. Then the zip. Then nothing.

I stood there with shampoo in my hair waiting for the crying. It didn't come. My shoulders came down from around my ears.

I put the conditioner in and left it for as long as the bottle says, which I have never done in my life. Then I rinsed it out with the water as hot as I like it.

That was five weeks ago. Now when the shower goes on, Theo goes to his mat. The TV still goes on some mornings too, and that's fine.

Ten minutes. That's all it is. But I come out of that bathroom able to think, and I'm nicer to him at 7:15 than I was all year.

And when I open the door, he holds up the laces to show me. I actually get to miss him a little. I hadn't been able to do that in seven months.

If you've got a small shadow who can't let you out of his sight, he's not too clingy and you're not doing anything wrong. He's just following the only thing in the house that moves.

I've written this out because a few friends asked what changed. 👇

You might get to the conditioner. ❤️

bodyText:
I was the one who made my husband's shed off limits to our grandson. I will own that.

Saws, jars of screws, forty years of tools.
It seemed obvious.

Then one Sunday I came down the garden and found this.

Frank's old toolbox, open on the bench, both clasps undone.
Our grandson's boots kicked off by the door, because Pop takes his off.

Frank had not let him near a single tool.
He had taken everything sharp out of that toolbox and handed it over, just for the clasps.

"The apprentice," he calls him now.

It took me a while to understand what Frank had seen in that boy.

It started at our back gate. But first, a little about us.

My name is Nancy. I am seventy-one. After Sunday dinner, my daughter Anne and her husband Michael go for a long walk, the one hour of the week they get to themselves.

Our grandson Thomas, who is two and a half, stays with Frank and me.

For a long time, I will be honest, we did not know what to do with him.

Frank was a tradesman for forty-three years. He can rehang a door with his eyes shut. But put him in a room with a two year old and no instructions, and he goes quiet. He said it to me more than once, drying the plates. "I don't know what to do with him, Nance."

So after pudding, Thomas would drift to the television, and one of us would put something on for him.

I am not against the television. There are afternoons I am glad of it.

But there is one Sunday last winter I have not forgotten. I came in from the kitchen and Frank was asleep in his armchair, the television going, and Thomas was on the rug in front of it, perfectly still.

I stood in the doorway with the tea towel and thought, this is not what I imagined. I had pictured these afternoons for years. They did not look like this.

So we tried.

🧸 The girls' old toys, kept thirty years in the spare room. He tipped them out and went back to the television.
🌳 The park. Frank's knee managed twenty minutes and complained about it until Wednesday.
🚜 A ride-on digger Frank chose himself. Thomas sat on it twice. It went to the shed, where it lives with the lawnmower.

One night I typed "what to do with a toddler at grandparents house" into my iPad. It was all craft projects. Glitter, mostly.

In the end it was Frank who worked it out, and he was not even trying.

One mild Sunday in March, Thomas followed him out to the timber gate by the vegetable bed and found the latch. It is an old metal thumb latch, right at his height.

He lifted it. The gate swung. He shut it, and it clicked. He lifted it again.

Frank, who knows exactly what that gate needs, which is nothing, took a screwdriver out of his pocket and pretended to fix the top hinge so he could stay out there with him.

I watched from the kitchen window with my hands in the sink.

Thomas opened and shut that gate for forty minutes. I know it was forty, because Frank timed it on his watch, and when they came in he wrote it in the little notebook he keeps in his shirt pocket.

Then he sat down at the kitchen table, took his glasses off, and said, "The boy wants a job, Nance. Not a toy."

When I looked around our house with it in mind, I saw what Thomas sees. The china cabinet, look, don't touch. Frank's tools, not for little hands. My sewing basket. The good ornaments. Everything in a grandparent's house belongs to somebody, and it is never him. The television was the only thing in our sitting room nobody said no to.

He was not choosing the television. It was all that was left.

What he needed was the gate, brought inside. Something with real latches and buckles and zips, that was properly his, and that Frank could do with him from his armchair, knee and all.

And here is the part I am a little embarrassed by. We already had one.

I keep a soft felt board for Thomas at dinner. It folds shut like a book, with buckles, zips, laces and little latches on its pages. I had always thought of it as a dinner thing, and after pudding it went back in the sideboard with the good napkins.

That Sunday, Frank asked for it.

Now it comes out after dinner. Frank sits in his armchair, Thomas on the footstool at his knee, a page across both their laps. Frank calls him the apprentice and gives him his jobs in the voice he used on building sites. "That buckle's not done up, apprentice." Thomas does it up, and holds it high to be inspected.

The pages come off, so Frank hands them over like jobs on a list.

Nobody falls asleep in that armchair anymore, not until Thomas has gone home.

The television still goes on sometimes, while Anne packs the car. I do not mind it at all.

But last Sunday Thomas came in, walked straight past it, and went to the sideboard. "Pop," he said. "Job."

Frank has had a lot of titles in his life. I do not think any of them pleased him more.

I have written my list out, the things we keep at our house for him now. It is linked below.

And if you never buy a thing, find him a latch this Sunday. A gate, a toolbox, a cupboard you do not mind him opening. Give him the job of it, and stay out there with him.
