bodyText:
I took this photo in the middle of the biggest meeting I'd had all year.

I was muted. Again.

That little red microphone was the only thing in my house I had any control over that morning.

The toast is from 7am. I never got back to it.

And down at the edge of the table, that's her hand. Reaching for my arm, for the third time in about a minute.

I sent it to my husband with no caption. He wrote back "oh no."

He didn't know the worst part hadn't happened yet. Neither did I.

It happened with that microphone switched on.

Let me back up.

I had a presentation at 10am that Friday.

I'd been building it for two weeks. It was the first big thing I'd been handed since going back after she was born, and I'm good at my job. I wanted them to see that I still was.

Then daycare sent a reminder that they were closed Friday for a staff day. It had been on the fridge for a month. I'd missed it.

My daughter is two and a half. My husband couldn't move his day. So it was me, her, and the laptop on the kitchen table.

I put her show on in the next room and it looped the whole morning. I presented my numbers over the same song coming through the wall.

I muted myself 11 times. I know because I started counting at five.

Halfway through the slide I'd worked hardest on, she climbed the back of my chair. On camera. A small striped sock came over my shoulder while I was talking about the budget.

Then she was pulling at my arm, and I turned and hissed "please, just five minutes" through my teeth. A voice I would never use on anyone at work.

My camera was on. So was my mic.

There was a pause that felt very long. Then my manager said, really kindly, "We can do this another time."

I closed the laptop and sat there with both hands flat on the lid, face burning.

It wasn't that she'd interrupted. Everyone's kid interrupts. It was that my whole team had just heard me plead with a two-year-old. And I'd heard it too.

That night at 11:40pm I was lying in bed typing "how to work from home with a toddler" and then "toddler interrupts every zoom call".

Everything it told me, I'd already tried:

🛏️ Book calls in nap time. She dropped her nap two months ago.

🧶 A busy bag. I'd packed one that morning, pompoms and pipe cleaners in a zip bag. They were across the whole floor in 4 minutes.

🍎 Snacks at the desk. One bowl bought me one slide.

📱 The iPad. It honestly works, right up until the call ends and the fight to take it back starts. Some days that fight was longer than the call.

Every fix got me to the start of a call. None of them got me through one.

On Saturday morning I finally opened a message I'd been avoiding. Dana from my team, who has three kids, had written to me privately ten minutes after the meeting.

"Please don't feel bad about today. Mine did exactly that for years. Can I tell you what I worked out?"

She said her kids never came for the meeting. They came for her going still. On a call she sits down, goes quiet, stares at a screen, and stops doing anything a small person can see. She stops being interesting. And that's exactly when their hands run out of things to do.

I read it three times.

Because it was true. My daughter could play for ages while I unloaded the dishwasher. It was only ever when I sat down and went silent. The interruptions weren't following the call. They were following the stillness.

Dana had one rule. Before the laptop opens, something goes on the floor at her feet that has a lot of steps and makes no noise.

I had never once thought about the noise.

Hers was a soft felt busy board. Buckles, zips, laces, snaps, little velcro pieces. None of it makes a sound on a call.

I thought it looked a bit babyish. I ordered one anyway, because another closure day was on the calendar.

She had a cough the Tuesday it arrived, so she was home. At 9:55 I unzipped it under the desk and handed her the page with the buckles. Then I opened the laptop.

It was a 40 minute call. She came up once, to show me a buckle she'd done up by herself, then sat back down between my feet and started on the laces. I muted once. The cough was mine.

Now the board comes out when the laptop opens. She sees me sit down and goes to find it.

The TV still goes on some afternoons and I don't feel bad about it. This is just one more thing, and it's the one I reach for first on call days.

I gave that presentation two weeks later from the same kitchen table. She was underneath it doing the same buckle over and over, and I got to the last slide.

If she always seems to find you the second you go quiet, it isn't the call and it isn't you. You went still, and her hands ran out of things.

I've written up what Dana told me and linked the exact board below, because two people from that meeting have already asked. 👇

Even if you don't get this one, try putting something silent with lots of steps at your feet before your next call starts. Before, not during.

bodyText:
I took a photo of two empty coffee cups, and I'm not even slightly embarrassed about it.

Look at the bottoms of them.
Foam rings all the way down.
The lipstick on the rim is Claire's. The other cup is mine, and I drank every drop while it was warm.
One slice of cake, two forks, a couple of bites gone. We share now.
Both phones face down the whole time.
The sneaker at the edge is my daughter's, swinging off her chair while she worked on the board I'd brought for her.
That's the stroller handle next to it. We walked here.
We talked until the cups were empty, and I heard the end of every story.
Two months ago, a coffee with my oldest friend went very differently.

Jess has been my best friend since we were fourteen. She lives a flight away now, and two months ago she flew in for one day, just to see me.

We met at the café near my house at 10am. Me, Jess, and Mila, who is two.

We were there for 90 minutes. I did not finish one sentence.

Not one. Every time I got halfway, Mila needed something. Down from the chair. Back up. The sugar sachets. My spoon. My face, turned towards her with both her hands.

Jess was lovely about it. She'd start telling me about her new job and I'd say "sorry, keep going" and she'd say "no, it's fine," and neither of us ever found where she'd stopped.

My latte went cold with the heart still on top.

At the door I hugged her and said "sorry, next time properly."

She said "of course, love you."

It was the kindest thing she could have said. That's why I cried at the first red light.

On the drive home I worked it out. I hadn't finished a conversation with another adult in two years. Not with anyone.

And the invitations had quietly stopped. Nobody fell out with me. The group chat just started making plans I found out about afterwards, from photos.

I didn't blame them. For two years I'd been the friend who says "next time properly."

That night I was in bed by 8:30 with my phone, typing "toddler interrupts every conversation" and then "how to have a coffee with a toddler".

Every answer said to teach her to wait her turn. She's two.

And I'd already tried everything I could think of:

🌳 The park instead of a café. Mila runs, I chase, my friend stands by the swings holding both coffees. We talk in twelve-second pieces.

📱 My phone propped against the sugar jar. Twenty quiet minutes, with me half-listening over a cartoon. I still do this in the car sometimes. Screens aren't the enemy. But I wasn't really at that table either.

🌙 Meeting after her bedtime. I'm asleep by 9. I tried twice and yawned through the second one.

🥛 Babycinos. Gone in two minutes. Then she wants mine.

Every fix bought me a few minutes. None of them bought me a conversation.

At 8:52 Jess texted. She's been a nanny for ten years, and I'd honestly forgotten, because to me she's just Jess.

"She's not being difficult. She's two, there's nothing for her hands, and we were doing the one thing she can't join."

I read it about six times.

Talking was the one thing at that table Mila couldn't be part of. Jess and I each had a cup to hold while we talked. Mila had nothing.

Of course she climbed into the middle of it. It was the only way in.

She wasn't interrupting us. She was trying to join.

Jess sent one more message. Give her something of her own to work on, right next to your cup. Lots of steps. Silent. She's busy with her thing while you do yours.

I thought it sounded nice and wouldn't last five minutes in a café. Mila gets bored of new toys before I've got the packaging in the bin.

Then Jess sent a photo of the one she takes to work. A soft felt busy board that zips shut like a book. Buckles, a zip, laces, snaps, little velcro pieces. No sound. The pages come off, so you can hand over one at a time.

I ordered one before I put my phone down.

The first test was a Thursday, with Claire, a friend from my old work I hadn't seen in over a year. I texted her "coffee? warning, Mila's coming."

Our drinks came. I unzipped the board and put one page next to my cup. The buckle page.

Mila clicked it shut. Opened it. Clicked it shut. Then the zip, then the laces, frowning at it like it was very important work.

Claire told me about her sister's wedding. The whole thing, start to finish.

I heard the ending.

Then I told her something, and I finished it. Then I drank my latte, and it was still warm, and I nearly cried into it.

That was seven Thursdays ago. It's our standing coffee now. We share a slice of cake. Mila asks for "my work" when she sees me pick up my keys.

Jess is coming back next month. For the first time in two years, I'm not dreading the goodbye.

I don't think friends stop inviting you because they stop loving you. I think they stop because every visit ends with "next time properly."

Next time properly turned out to be a Thursday.

I've written the whole thing out because a few friends have asked since. 👇 The exact board is linked below if you want a look.

Even if you don't get this one, next time you meet a friend, put something on the table that's hers before the coffees come. You might hear the end of a story. ❤️

bodyText:
I took a photo of a full tissue box and nearly cried. I know how that sounds.

Look at it though.
Every tissue still in it.
Nobody pulled them out one at a time while I sat stuck under a feeding baby.
That's my tea beside it, drunk right to the bottom. While it was still hot.
The TV's off. All it's showing is the room.
The rug is just a rug again.
The feeding pillow's pushed aside because the feed is done. 40 minutes, and I didn't get up once.
My daughter spent the whole feed against my arm, doing up buckles on her board.
A few weeks ago this couch looked like a storm had been through it after every feed.
Let me go back to the start.

When Max was born, Evie was two and a half.

He feeds about eight times a day, 40 minutes each. For the first two weeks she kissed his head every morning like he was a present someone had left for her.

Then she worked out what a feed means.

It means mommy sits down and can't get up.

So every feed, she found something. She climbed the back of the couch. She opened the fridge and stood in it. She drew on the hallway wall, low down, right where I could see it and couldn't reach it. She pulled every tissue out of the box, one at a time, looking at me the whole way.

Eight times a day. I started to dread the little snuffling noises Max makes when he's hungry, because I knew what came next.

Everyone said she's jealous, it's normal, you ride it out. So I rode it out, and tried everything else too:

🧺 The special feeding-time basket, with books and toys that only came out for feeds. Tipped onto the rug in about three minutes, and she was back on the couch arm.

👶 "Involve her." She fetched me a nappy once, so proud of herself, and that job lasted one minute. That left 39 minutes of the feed.

🍎 A snack at every feed. She ate it. Then she wouldn't touch her dinner.

📺 The TV at every feed. It worked, I won't pretend it didn't. But eight feeds a day is a lot of TV, and I could feel it adding up in both of us.

Then one afternoon in week four, I was pinned in the corner of the couch halfway through a feed, and it went quiet. I leaned over as far as I could without unlatching him. The nappy cream. The whole tube, smeared into the cushions in big white handprints.

I didn't yell. I just cried. Sat there with the baby still feeding and cried where she could see me.

And she came over, climbed up next to me, put her face right up close to mine and said, "Mommy sad?"

That undid me. She wasn't trying to be bad. She was right there, worried about me, and I'd spent weeks thinking of her as the problem.

That night at 2:10am, feeding again, I typed "toddler acting out while I feed the baby" and then "toddler jealous of newborn". Every answer said extra attention, one-on-one time, be patient.

I was never alone with her. That was the whole problem.

At the six-week home visit, the child health nurse sat on our ottoman with her notes while I fed Max. Evie did her whole routine. Up the couch. Down. Tissue box. Fridge door.

The nurse watched the entire feed and didn't write a thing. Then she said, "She's not jealous of the baby. She's jealous of your hands."

I laughed. Then I couldn't stop thinking about it.

For 40 minutes, my hands are full and hers are empty. Every other part of the day I'm her climbing frame, her helper, her toy. The feed is the one time I can't be. So her hands go looking for something, and what's in reach is the fridge and the wall.

Nothing I'd tried lasted as long as a feed.

She needed a job that was only hers, right next to me, with enough steps to outlast her brother.

I figured that works on other people's kids. I ordered a pink felt busy board anyway. A soft one that zips shut like a book, with buckles, zips, laces and snaps across the pages.

One rule. It comes out when the feeding pillow comes out, and goes away when the pillow does. It's not an anytime toy. It's her feed job.

The first feed, she did the buckle page, then undid every lace, then asked me to do them back up so she could undo them again. Max finished. I looked at the clock. She hadn't left the couch once.

That was three weeks ago.

Now when Max makes his hungry noises, Evie says "baby's hungry" and goes to get her board. She sits against my arm and works through the pages while he feeds. Sometimes she tells him about it. "Max. Buckle. Click."

I get to look at both of them. I drink my water while it's still cold. Some feeds I actually close my eyes.

The TV still goes on some afternoons when I'm wrecked. It's just not eight times a day anymore, and I'm not crying on the couch.

If you're feeding a newborn while your toddler climbs the walls: she isn't being naughty, and you're not doing it wrong. Her hands just have nothing to do at the one time yours can't help.

I've written it all out because a few moms asked. 👇 The exact board is linked below if you want a look.

Even if you skip this one, try giving her one job tomorrow that only comes out at feed time. It might get you through a whole feed. 🤍

bodyText:
My daughter turned 2 with only 6 words. 

I cut screens. I bought flashcards. I played Ms. Rachel in the car until I wanted to drive into a lake.

I tried narrating my entire day out loud like a crazy person. 

I tried counting to 10 in my head every time she pointed at something before I would hand it to her. Just hoping she'd try to say the word. She never did.

And the scariest part was that she understood everything.

She just couldn't say anything back.

And I took it personally. Every single day.

Because if she understands me, and I'm doing everything the articles and the pediatricians and the Instagram speech therapists tell me to do, and she's still not talking — who else is there to blame except me?

I brought it up at her 2 year checkup.

I told the pediatrician I was worried. I told her my daughter barely had any words and that nothing I was doing seemed to help.

She looked at her chart and said "she's still within range. Some kids just take a little longer. Let's revisit at 2 and a half."

I cried in the car before I drove home.

I went in hoping for answers and came out with the same thing everyone keeps telling me. Wait.

My husband told me the same thing that night. "The doctor said she's fine. You're overthinking this."

So I stopped talking about it.

But I didn't stop thinking about it.

Every day I watched her and I knew. She wasn't catching up. She wasn't "getting there." 

She was stuck. And so was I.

I called the pediatrician back and asked for a speech therapy referral.

The waitlist was 5 months.

And I knew I couldn't sit there for 5 months doing nothing. 

So I did what I always do when I can't sleep and I can't fix something. I got on my phone.

I spent weeks reading everything I could find. 

Articles. Reddit threads. Posts from speech pathologists. 

Most of it was the same advice I'd already been doing. 

“Narrate your day. Read at bedtime. Cut screens. Label everything.”

I wanted to throw my phone at the wall. Because I’d been doing all of that for a year and nothing changed.

But I didn’t give up on a solution. So I kept reading. 

And a few nights later, I found a comment from a speech pathologist that changed everything. 

She wasn't selling anything. She was just answering a mom who was in the same spot as me.

And she said something that stopped me cold.

She said "your daughter doesn't need to hear more words. She needs to produce them. Everything you're doing right now — the reading, the narrating, the labeling — she's on the receiving end of all of it. She's listening. But she's not doing. And kids don't learn to talk by listening. They learn by trying. Over and over. On their own. Without pressure."

I sat there staring at my phone in the dark.

Because she just described why nothing I tried was working.

Every single thing I had been doing, my daughter was on the receiving end. 

I was the one talking. I was the one reading. I was the one narrating, labeling, and pointing.

She was just sitting there absorbing it. None of it was actually getting her to open her mouth and speak.

So it wasn't that I didn’t try hard enough. It was that I was trying the wrong things.

The speech pathologist in that thread called it cause-and-effect play. She said it's the number one technique used in speech therapy clinics. 

The child presses something, hears a word, and tries to repeat it. 

No adult hovering. No pressure. Just repetition at their own pace. 

I had never given my daughter a single chance to do that at home. 

So I started looking for something that would let her.

I read through the rest of the comments. And somewhere near the bottom, there was a mom who mentioned a sound book that her speech therapist had recommended.

She said her son used it for a few weeks and started saying new words on his own.

I almost scrolled past it. Because I'd been down that road before. I'd already spent hundreds of dollars on toys and apps and flashcards that were collecting dust.

But it was $50. And I was desperate. 

So I ordered it.

The first week I didn't see much. She pressed a few buttons. Wandered off. I thought here we go again.

But by week two she started pulling it off the shelf on her own after breakfast. I didn't ask her to. 

I didn't put it in front of her. She just went and got it.

There's a game mode where the book says a word and she has to find the matching picture and repeat the word. She got hooked on that. She'd play it over and over.

By week three I heard her making sounds along with the book. Quiet little attempts. Not real words yet. But her mouth was doing something it had never done before.

And for the first time in a year I didn't feel like I was failing her.

I wasn't standing over her begging her to say a word. 

She was choosing to sit with the book and try. On her own terms.

About a month in I was folding laundry in the next room and I heard her say "dog."

Not to me. To the book. 

I walked in and stood in the doorway and watched her. 

She pressed the picture of the cat. The book said "cat." She said "cah." 

She pressed the cow. The book said "cow." She said "cow."

I put my hand over my mouth and I just stood there.

That was the first time in her entire life she had tried to say words without me asking her to.

Two weeks after that she pointed at her cup and said "juice."

She didn't cry. She didn't whine. She didn't drag me to the fridge. She just said it.

I handed it to her and turned around so she wouldn't see me crying.

After that it started happening every day. New words. Some clear. Some garbled. Some barely attempts. But she was trying. Every single day she was trying.

Her daycare teacher pulled me aside at pickup and told me her language had exploded. 

She said she barely recognized her from a few months ago, and that she was starting to talk to the other kids.

We went back for her 2 and a half year checkup.

Same pediatrician. Same office.

She'd gone from 6 words to over 50.

The pediatrician started going through her usual checklist. 

She held up a picture of a dog to see if my daughter would point to it. 

My daughter looked at it and said "doggy." 

The pediatrician looked at me over her glasses and said "well that's new."

Then my daughter looked at the pediatrician and said "what's new?" 

The pediatrician put her pen down and just looked at me.

She said we didn't need speech therapy anymore.

She wrote down the name of the sound book and just nodded.

My husband was quiet on the drive home. But after she went to sleep that night, he sat next to me on the couch and said "I should have listened to you."

And I'll be honest. That felt good. 

But it wasn't the most important thing to me.

The part that mattered was that I stopped blaming myself.

For a year I had been carrying around this weight that I was the reason my daughter wasn't talking. That I was doing something wrong. That if I were a better mom she'd be talking by now.

But that wasn’t true. 

I wasn't doing anything wrong. I  just needed to give her a different method. 

And this book proved that.

It was designed by speech pathologists. It has 500 clearly spoken words in it.

Every page has a red start button and icons she could press to hear each word.

There were themed pages for feelings, food, animals, family, body parts, etc. 

It had all the words she needed to learn how to say. 23 themed worlds in total.

And she had free access to any of them whenever she wanted just by pressing a button.

Which is the part I didn't realize was so important until the speech pathologist said it.

My daughter was in control. She decided when to press it, which words to hear, and how many times to hear it.

That's when kids actually learn. When they're the one driving it. 

Not when we're standing over them begging,

There's also a phonics mode where the book teaches each letter's sound.

So beyond learning words she was starting to piece together how they were built.

It's screen-free and USB-C rechargeable so we're not fighting over dead batteries.

And the pages are thick and tear-proof so she can't rip them no matter how rough she plays with it.

And unlike an iPad, when she's done with it she's calm. 

Not amped up. Not melting down.

It's the only thing that finally worked.

I'm not saying it’s a miracle. I'm not saying it will work for every kid overnight.

But I'm saying if you're where I was — doing everything right and still watching your kid fall behind — it might not be you. It might be the method.

This book gave my daughter something I couldn't give her no matter how hard I tried. 

A way to practice on her own.

The link is below if you want to check it out. They are running a sale right now.

P.S. — I'm not a speech pathologist. I'm just a mom who spent a year blaming herself before she realized the problem was never her. If your child has been evaluated and is in therapy, keep doing that. This isn't a replacement for professional help. It's the thing that finally made everything click at home when nothing else would.

bodyText:
I took this photo so I'd stop telling people my mornings were fine.

That's my coffee, sitting in the microwave, at 5:34am.
First reheat of the day.
There would be three more.

The green clock is the only light on in the kitchen.
I don't turn the big lights on. It feels like admitting the day has started.

In the next room the TV had just gone on.
Same minute as yesterday.
Same minute as every day.

I'm not posting this for sympathy.
I'm posting it because I think a lot of us are standing in dark kitchens right now, and nobody really says so.

Everyone talks about the witching hour at 5pm. Nobody talks about 5:30am.

My son Hudson is two. He wakes at 5:20. Every day. Weekends too.

My partner leaves for work at 6. From 5:20 it's the two of us, a dark house, and a long stretch until anything opens.

For about eight months, the TV went on at 5:34. Same minute every morning. Change him, milk, couch, remote.

Then I'd make a coffee and put it down somewhere. Microwave it. Forget it. Microwave it again. I once found it in there at lunchtime, full, after its fourth go.

I haven't had a hot coffee in over a year. I know how small that sounds.

One morning I looked up from the couch and the sky outside was pink. The TV had been on for 90 minutes before it was even light.

I sat there with a cold mug and tried to remember the last morning I'd actually been awake for. Not getting through it. Awake.

I couldn't.

The sun had come up and I'd missed it again. It came up every day while I was on the couch watching a cartoon I could recite.

That night at 9:40 I typed "toddler wakes at 5am what to do". Then "how to entertain toddler early morning".

Almost every answer was about getting him to wake later. Blackout blinds (have them). Move bedtime (tried both ways, still 5:20).

Nobody answered the question I asked. He's up. Now what?

And I'd already tried:

🧸 A basket of toys by his cot. Thrown over the rail, one by one, by 5:25.

📺 The TV. It worked. Quiet till 7. Then by 8 he was climbing the back of the couch.

🍌 Breakfast at 5:30. Hungry again at 7. Two breakfasts before daylight.

🛋️ Me lying on the rug "resting my eyes" while he climbed me like a hill.

Every fix got me to 6. None of them got me a coffee.

Then my dad came to stay for a week.

Dad was a baker for 38 years, up at 4am his whole working life. On his first morning, when Hudson came out at 5:20, Dad was already at the kitchen table.

I went to put the TV on and he said, "Leave it a sec."

He'd tipped out my kitchen drawer. A zip-up pencil case, a lunchbox with clip lids. Hudson climbed onto a chair and went at it. Zip, unzip. Clip, unclip.

I stood there holding the remote like an idiot.

Later I asked Dad how he knew. He shrugged and said, "Nobody wakes up wanting to watch. They wake up wanting to do."

Then he told me about the bakery. Every night before he went home, he set out the first job for the morning. Tins greased, flour weighed, bench clear. So at 4am his hands had somewhere to go before his head was awake.

Hudson's hands wake up before the house does. At 5:20 everything in our house is off, put away, quiet. The only thing in the house that's "on" is the TV. Of course that's where our mornings went.

He wasn't asking to watch. He was asking for something to do, and nobody had left him anything.

After Dad left, the kitchen drawer got old fast. I wanted one thing I could set out the night before, quiet at 5:30am, with enough jobs in it to last. I ended up with a soft felt busy board that folds shut like a book and zips closed. Felt pages inside, with buckles, zips, laces, latches, snaps. No sound, no lights, nothing to switch on.

I thought it looked too simple.

That night I left it zipped on the couch, next to my coffee spot, right where he lands.

5:20, the monitor. 5:24, he's on the couch. He found the zip before I'd filled the kettle. I heard the buckle click in the quiet, then again, then the zip.

I drank that coffee hot. Standing at the counter, burning my lip a little. I actually laughed.

It's been six weeks. He still wakes at 5:20, and I've made my peace with that. What's changed is what 5:30 looks like. He unzips his board. I make my coffee. Some mornings we sit by the window and watch the sky go pink, and he points at it like he made it.

The TV still goes on some mornings. Just later, and not because it's the only thing in the house that's on.

5:30 to 7 is 90 minutes a day. That's over ten hours a week I was spending just getting through.

If your mornings start in the dark too, your kid isn't difficult and you're not doing anything wrong. His hands are awake, and nobody's given them anything yet.

I've written it all out because a couple of the moms at daycare asked what changed. 👇 The exact board is linked below if you want a look.

Even if you don't get this one, tonight, leave something out for his hands right where he lands. You might drink your coffee hot tomorrow. ☕

bodyText:
I let him bring half the house into the bathroom, because it was the only way he'd stop crying.

This is the bath mat outside our shower on a normal morning.

A toy truck. My hairbrush. The TV remote. His sippy cup. One sock, which never did find its other half.

He'd carry things in one at a time while I showered. Drop them on the mat. Go and get more.

Anything to be in the room with me.

I'd step out dripping and pick my way through it.

It sounds sweet. And it was, a bit.

It was also the only way I got to shower at all.

My son Theo is two. For seven months, I did not shower alone once.

My partner Dan leaves for work at 5:30, so mornings are just us. The second the bathroom door clicks shut, Theo is on the other side.

First the knocking. Then "Mama? Mama?" Then four little fingers under the door, checking I'm still in there.

Then the crying.

I got fast. Shampoo in, shampoo out. Conditioner went in and stayed in, because rinsing it meant another minute of him sobbing at the door.

I told myself it was a phase. Just who he is. Some kids are cuddly. Mine was velcro.

Then one Thursday I turned the shower on, wrapped myself in a towel and sat down on the closed toilet lid.

I left the water running so he'd think I was busy.

I just wanted two minutes where nobody was touching me. So I sat there in a towel, hiding from my own son, listening to him cry through the door.

I hated myself for it.

That night at 11:40 I was in bed typing "toddler won't let me leave the room" into my phone. Then "2 year old follows me everywhere".

I'd already tried most of what came up:

🚧 A playpen outside the bathroom door. He stood at the bars and screamed my name instead.

🧺 A special bathroom toy basket. Two good mornings, then he was back at the door.

🚿 Bringing him in the shower with me. I spent the whole time stopping him slipping on the tiles. Very clean toddler. Still unwashed mom.

📺 The TV on in the next room. Four minutes, then he came looking for me.

😢 "Just let him cry, he'll learn." He didn't. I did. I learned to wash my hair faster.

Every one of them moved the crying somewhere else. None of them stopped it.

Then one Tuesday, he went quiet.

Twelve minutes of quiet outside the door. With a two year old that's scarier than crying, so I got out dripping and opened it.

He'd found my makeup bag. He was sitting on the carpet zipping it open and shut. Open, shut, open, shut. Lids off my lipsticks and back on. A mascara, a hair clip and a tiny mirror lined up in a row, then all over again.

He didn't even look up at me.

I stood there in my towel and it finally made sense.

It was never about me leaving. Everything in our house is exactly where it was yesterday. His toys do the same thing every time. Then there's me. Water running, drawers opening, things going on and coming off. I'm the only thing in the house that keeps changing.

So he follows me. Little hands with nothing new go looking for the one thing that changes.

That makeup bag had a next thing. A zip, then a lid, then a row to make. Every time he finished something, something else was waiting.

So I stopped trying to get him away from the door, and started putting something with a next step right where he lands.

I didn't think a toy stood a chance. He'd walked past every toy we own to sit against that door.

But I found a soft felt busy board that folds shut like a book. Every page is a different job. A buckle, then a zip, then laces, then shapes to match.

I put a spare bath mat in the hallway, right where he always sits, and opened the board on it.

First morning, I heard his fingers under the door once. Then a click. Then the zip. Then nothing.

I stood there with shampoo in my hair waiting for the crying. It didn't come. My shoulders came down from around my ears.

I put the conditioner in and left it for as long as the bottle says, which I have never done in my life. Then I rinsed it out with the water as hot as I like it.

That was five weeks ago. Now when the shower goes on, Theo goes to his mat. The TV still goes on some mornings too, and that's fine.

Ten minutes. That's all it is. But I come out of that bathroom able to think, and I'm nicer to him at 7:15 than I was all year.

And when I open the door, he holds up the laces to show me. I actually get to miss him a little. I hadn't been able to do that in seven months.

If you've got a small shadow who can't let you out of his sight, he's not too clingy and you're not doing anything wrong. He's just following the only thing in the house that moves.

I've written this out because a few friends asked what changed. 👇

The exact board is linked below if you want a look. Even if you don't get this one, try leaving something with a zip or a buckle outside the bathroom door tomorrow and see what he does.

You might get to the conditioner. ❤️

bodyText:
My daughter turned 2 with only 6 words. 

I cut screens. I bought flashcards. I played Ms. Rachel in the car until I wanted to drive into a lake.

I tried narrating my entire day out loud like a crazy person. 

I tried counting to 10 in my head every time she pointed at something before I would hand it to her. Just hoping she'd try to say the word. She never did.

And the scariest part was that she understood everything.

She just couldn't say anything back.

And I took it personally. Every single day.

Because if she understands me, and I'm doing everything the articles and the pediatricians and the Instagram speech therapists tell me to do, and she's still not talking — who else is there to blame except me?

I brought it up at her 2 year checkup.

I told the pediatrician I was worried. I told her my daughter barely had any words and that nothing I was doing seemed to help.

She looked at her chart and said "she's still within range. Some kids just take a little longer. Let's revisit at 2 and a half."

I cried in the car before I drove home.

I went in hoping for answers and came out with the same thing everyone keeps telling me. Wait.

My husband told me the same thing that night. "The doctor said she's fine. You're overthinking this."

So I stopped talking about it.

But I didn't stop thinking about it.

Every day I watched her and I knew. She wasn't catching up. She wasn't "getting there." 

She was stuck. And so was I.

I called the pediatrician back and asked for a speech therapy referral.

The waitlist was 5 months.

And I knew I couldn't sit there for 5 months doing nothing. 

So I did what I always do when I can't sleep and I can't fix something. I got on my phone.

I spent weeks reading everything I could find. 

Articles. Reddit threads. Posts from speech pathologists. 

Most of it was the same advice I'd already been doing. 

“Narrate your day. Read at bedtime. Cut screens. Label everything.”

I wanted to throw my phone at the wall. Because I’d been doing all of that for a year and nothing changed.

But I didn’t give up on a solution. So I kept reading. 

And a few nights later, I found a comment from a speech pathologist that changed everything. 

She wasn't selling anything. She was just answering a mom who was in the same spot as me.

And she said something that stopped me cold.

She said "your daughter doesn't need to hear more words. She needs to produce them. Everything you're doing right now — the reading, the narrating, the labeling — she's on the receiving end of all of it. She's listening. But she's not doing. And kids don't learn to talk by listening. They learn by trying. Over and over. On their own. Without pressure."

I sat there staring at my phone in the dark.

Because she just described why nothing I tried was working.

Every single thing I had been doing, my daughter was on the receiving end. 

I was the one talking. I was the one reading. I was the one narrating, labeling, and pointing.

She was just sitting there absorbing it. None of it was actually getting her to open her mouth and speak.

So it wasn't that I didn’t try hard enough. It was that I was trying the wrong things.

The speech pathologist in that thread called it cause-and-effect play. She said it's the number one technique used in speech therapy clinics. 

The child presses something, hears a word, and tries to repeat it. 

No adult hovering. No pressure. Just repetition at their own pace. 

I had never given my daughter a single chance to do that at home. 

So I started looking for something that would let her.

I read through the rest of the comments. And somewhere near the bottom, there was a mom who mentioned a sound book that her speech therapist had recommended.

She said her son used it for a few weeks and started saying new words on his own.

I almost scrolled past it. Because I'd been down that road before. I'd already spent hundreds of dollars on toys and apps and flashcards that were collecting dust.

But it was $50. And I was desperate. 

So I ordered it.

The first week I didn't see much. She pressed a few buttons. Wandered off. I thought here we go again.

But by week two she started pulling it off the shelf on her own after breakfast. I didn't ask her to. 

I didn't put it in front of her. She just went and got it.

There's a game mode where the book says a word and she has to find the matching picture and repeat the word. She got hooked on that. She'd play it over and over.

By week three I heard her making sounds along with the book. Quiet little attempts. Not real words yet. But her mouth was doing something it had never done before.

And for the first time in a year I didn't feel like I was failing her.

I wasn't standing over her begging her to say a word. 

She was choosing to sit with the book and try. On her own terms.

About a month in I was folding laundry in the next room and I heard her say "dog."

Not to me. To the book. 

I walked in and stood in the doorway and watched her. 

She pressed the picture of the cat. The book said "cat." She said "cah." 

She pressed the cow. The book said "cow." She said "cow."

I put my hand over my mouth and I just stood there.

That was the first time in her entire life she had tried to say words without me asking her to.

Two weeks after that she pointed at her cup and said "juice."

She didn't cry. She didn't whine. She didn't drag me to the fridge. She just said it.

I handed it to her and turned around so she wouldn't see me crying.

After that it started happening every day. New words. Some clear. Some garbled. Some barely attempts. But she was trying. Every single day she was trying.

Her daycare teacher pulled me aside at pickup and told me her language had exploded. 

She said she barely recognized her from a few months ago, and that she was starting to talk to the other kids.

We went back for her 2 and a half year checkup.

Same pediatrician. Same office.

She'd gone from 6 words to over 50.

The pediatrician started going through her usual checklist. 

She held up a picture of a dog to see if my daughter would point to it. 

My daughter looked at it and said "doggy." 

The pediatrician looked at me over her glasses and said "well that's new."

Then my daughter looked at the pediatrician and said "what's new?" 

The pediatrician put her pen down and just looked at me.

She said we didn't need speech therapy anymore.

She wrote down the name of the sound book and just nodded.

My husband was quiet on the drive home. But after she went to sleep that night, he sat next to me on the couch and said "I should have listened to you."

And I'll be honest. That felt good. 

But it wasn't the most important thing to me.

The part that mattered was that I stopped blaming myself.

For a year I had been carrying around this weight that I was the reason my daughter wasn't talking. That I was doing something wrong. That if I were a better mom she'd be talking by now.

But that wasn’t true. 

I wasn't doing anything wrong. I  just needed to give her a different method. 

And this book proved that.

It was designed by speech pathologists. It has 500 clearly spoken words in it.

Every page has a red start button and icons she could press to hear each word.

There were themed pages for feelings, food, animals, family, body parts, etc. 

It had all the words she needed to learn how to say. 23 themed worlds in total.

And she had free access to any of them whenever she wanted just by pressing a button.

Which is the part I didn't realize was so important until the speech pathologist said it.

My daughter was in control. She decided when to press it, which words to hear, and how many times to hear it.

That's when kids actually learn. When they're the one driving it. 

Not when we're standing over them begging,

There's also a phonics mode where the book teaches each letter's sound.

So beyond learning words she was starting to piece together how they were built.

It's screen-free and USB-C rechargeable so we're not fighting over dead batteries.

And the pages are thick and tear-proof so she can't rip them no matter how rough she plays with it.

And unlike an iPad, when she's done with it she's calm. 

Not amped up. Not melting down.

It's the only thing that finally worked.

I'm not saying it’s a miracle. I'm not saying it will work for every kid overnight.

But I'm saying if you're where I was — doing everything right and still watching your kid fall behind — it might not be you. It might be the method.

This book gave my daughter something I couldn't give her no matter how hard I tried. 

A way to practice on her own.

bodyText:
For two years I've been the friend who texts "sorry we didn't really get to talk."

This is my phone on the passenger seat, about four minutes after I said goodbye to my best friend.
She'd flown in for one day to see me.
She texted first. "so good to see you!!"
I wrote the middle one with my daughter kicking the back of my seat.
Then she replied. "haha next time properly. love you"
She'd already said the same thing at the door.
She's the kindest person I know, and she wasn't wrong about any of it.
I just sat there looking at it with the keys in my hand.

Jess has been my best friend since we were fourteen. She lives a flight away now, and two months ago she flew in for one day, just to see me.

We met at the café near my house at 10am. Me, Jess, and Mila, who is two.

We were there for 90 minutes. I did not finish one sentence.

Not one. Every time I got halfway, Mila needed something. Down from the chair. Back up. The sugar sachets. My spoon. My face, turned towards her with both her hands.

Jess was lovely about it. She'd start telling me about her new job and I'd say "sorry, keep going" and she'd say "no, it's fine," and neither of us ever found where she'd stopped.

My latte went cold with the heart still on top.

At the door I hugged her and said "sorry, next time properly."

She said "of course, love you."

It was the kindest thing she could have said. That's why I cried at the first red light.

On the drive home I worked it out. I hadn't finished a conversation with another adult in two years. Not with anyone.

And the invitations had quietly stopped. Nobody fell out with me. The group chat just started making plans I found out about afterwards, from photos.

I didn't blame them. For two years I'd been the friend who says "next time properly."

That night I was in bed by 8:30 with my phone, typing "toddler interrupts every conversation" and then "how to have a coffee with a toddler".

Every answer said to teach her to wait her turn. She's two.

And I'd already tried everything I could think of:

🌳 The park instead of a café. Mila runs, I chase, my friend stands by the swings holding both coffees. We talk in twelve-second pieces.

📱 My phone propped against the sugar jar. Twenty quiet minutes, with me half-listening over a cartoon. I still do this in the car sometimes. Screens aren't the enemy. But I wasn't really at that table either.

🌙 Meeting after her bedtime. I'm asleep by 9. I tried twice and yawned through the second one.

🥛 Babycinos. Gone in two minutes. Then she wants mine.

Every fix bought me a few minutes. None of them bought me a conversation.

At 8:52 Jess texted. She's been a nanny for ten years, and I'd honestly forgotten, because to me she's just Jess.

"She's not being difficult. She's two, there's nothing for her hands, and we were doing the one thing she can't join."

I read it about six times.

Talking was the one thing at that table Mila couldn't be part of. Jess and I each had a cup to hold while we talked. Mila had nothing.

Of course she climbed into the middle of it. It was the only way in.

She wasn't interrupting us. She was trying to join.

Jess sent one more message. Give her something of her own to work on, right next to your cup. Lots of steps. Silent. She's busy with her thing while you do yours.

I thought it sounded nice and wouldn't last five minutes in a café. Mila gets bored of new toys before I've got the packaging in the bin.

Then Jess sent a photo of the one she takes to work. A soft felt busy board that zips shut like a book. Buckles, a zip, laces, snaps, little velcro pieces. No sound. The pages come off, so you can hand over one at a time.

I ordered one before I put my phone down.

The first test was a Thursday, with Claire, a friend from my old work I hadn't seen in over a year. I texted her "coffee? warning, Mila's coming."

Our drinks came. I unzipped the board and put one page next to my cup. The buckle page.

Mila clicked it shut. Opened it. Clicked it shut. Then the zip, then the laces, frowning at it like it was very important work.

Claire told me about her sister's wedding. The whole thing, start to finish.

I heard the ending.

Then I told her something, and I finished it. Then I drank my latte, and it was still warm, and I nearly cried into it.

That was seven Thursdays ago. It's our standing coffee now. We share a slice of cake. Mila asks for "my work" when she sees me pick up my keys.

Jess is coming back next month. For the first time in two years, I'm not dreading the goodbye.

I don't think friends stop inviting you because they stop loving you. I think they stop because every visit ends with "next time properly."

Next time properly turned out to be a Thursday.

I've written the whole thing out because a few friends have asked since. 👇 The exact board is linked below if you want a look.

Even if you don't get this one, next time you meet a friend, put something on the table that's hers before the coffees come. You might hear the end of a story. ❤️

bodyText:
I nearly cried over a bottle of conditioner this morning. I know how that sounds.

This is our bathroom vanity, about ten minutes after I got in the shower.

That coffee was made before I turned the water on. It's still steaming.

That's the conditioner, cap still open. I used it. Left it in. Rinsed it out properly, with the water hot.

And that one streak wiped through the fog on the mirror is where I stood and looked at myself for longer than I have in months.

Through the door, the hallway is quiet. Just a spare bath mat and one little sock.

Nobody knocking. No fingers under the door.

For most of this year, that bottle barely moved.

My son Theo is two. For seven months, I did not shower alone once.

My partner Dan leaves for work at 5:30, so mornings are just us. The second the bathroom door clicks shut, Theo is on the other side.

First the knocking. Then "Mama? Mama?" Then four little fingers under the door, checking I'm still in there.

Then the crying.

I got fast. Shampoo in, shampoo out. Conditioner went in and stayed in, because rinsing it meant another minute of him sobbing at the door.

I told myself it was a phase. Just who he is. Some kids are cuddly. Mine was velcro.

Then one Thursday I turned the shower on, wrapped myself in a towel and sat down on the closed toilet lid.

I left the water running so he'd think I was busy.

I just wanted two minutes where nobody was touching me. So I sat there in a towel, hiding from my own son, listening to him cry through the door.

I hated myself for it.

That night at 11:40 I was in bed typing "toddler won't let me leave the room" into my phone. Then "2 year old follows me everywhere".

I'd already tried most of what came up:

🚧 A playpen outside the bathroom door. He stood at the bars and screamed my name instead.

🧺 A special bathroom toy basket. Two good mornings, then he was back at the door.

🚿 Bringing him in the shower with me. I spent the whole time stopping him slipping on the tiles. Very clean toddler. Still unwashed mom.

📺 The TV on in the next room. Four minutes, then he came looking for me.

😢 "Just let him cry, he'll learn." He didn't. I did. I learned to wash my hair faster.

Every one of them moved the crying somewhere else. None of them stopped it.

Then one Tuesday, he went quiet.

Twelve minutes of quiet outside the door. With a two year old that's scarier than crying, so I got out dripping and opened it.

He'd found my makeup bag. He was sitting on the carpet zipping it open and shut. Open, shut, open, shut. Lids off my lipsticks and back on. A mascara, a hair clip and a tiny mirror lined up in a row, then all over again.

He didn't even look up at me.

I stood there in my towel and it finally made sense.

It was never about me leaving. Everything in our house is exactly where it was yesterday. His toys do the same thing every time. Then there's me. Water running, drawers opening, things going on and coming off. I'm the only thing in the house that keeps changing.

So he follows me. Little hands with nothing new go looking for the one thing that changes.

That makeup bag had a next thing. A zip, then a lid, then a row to make. Every time he finished something, something else was waiting.

So I stopped trying to get him away from the door, and started putting something with a next step right where he lands.

I didn't think a toy stood a chance. He'd walked past every toy we own to sit against that door.

But I found a soft felt busy board that folds shut like a book. Every page is a different job. A buckle, then a zip, then laces, then shapes to match.

I put a spare bath mat in the hallway, right where he always sits, and opened the board on it.

First morning, I heard his fingers under the door once. Then a click. Then the zip. Then nothing.

I stood there with shampoo in my hair waiting for the crying. It didn't come. My shoulders came down from around my ears.

I put the conditioner in and left it for as long as the bottle says, which I have never done in my life. Then I rinsed it out with the water as hot as I like it.

That was five weeks ago. Now when the shower goes on, Theo goes to his mat. The TV still goes on some mornings too, and that's fine.

Ten minutes. That's all it is. But I come out of that bathroom able to think, and I'm nicer to him at 7:15 than I was all year.

And when I open the door, he holds up the laces to show me. I actually get to miss him a little. I hadn't been able to do that in seven months.

If you've got a small shadow who can't let you out of his sight, he's not too clingy and you're not doing anything wrong. He's just following the only thing in the house that moves.

I've written this out because a few friends asked what changed. 👇

The exact board is linked below if you want a look. Even if you don't get this one, try leaving something with a zip or a buckle outside the bathroom door tomorrow and see what he does.

You might get to the conditioner. ❤️

bodyText:
From the waist up in this photo, I'm presenting to my whole team in a nice top and earrings.

From the waist down, I'm in the bottoms I slept in.

And between my feet is my daughter, sitting in the middle of a busy bag I packed the night before.

Pompoms. Pipe cleaners. I'd found it on a list of ideas for working from home.

I took this 4 minutes after I tipped it out. A minute later she was trying to climb my leg.

I'm a bit embarrassed by how much hope I'd put in one zip bag.

That bag was plan A for the biggest morning I'd had at work all year.

I had a presentation at 10am that Friday.

I'd been building it for two weeks. It was the first big thing I'd been handed since going back after she was born, and I'm good at my job. I wanted them to see that I still was.

Then daycare sent a reminder that they were closed Friday for a staff day. It had been on the fridge for a month. I'd missed it.

My daughter is two and a half. My husband couldn't move his day. So it was me, her, and the laptop on the kitchen table.

I put her show on in the next room and it looped the whole morning. I presented my numbers over the same song coming through the wall.

I muted myself 11 times. I know because I started counting at five.

Halfway through the slide I'd worked hardest on, she climbed the back of my chair. On camera. A small striped sock came over my shoulder while I was talking about the budget.

Then she was pulling at my arm, and I turned and hissed "please, just five minutes" through my teeth. A voice I would never use on anyone at work.

My camera was on. So was my mic.

There was a pause that felt very long. Then my manager said, really kindly, "We can do this another time."

I closed the laptop and sat there with both hands flat on the lid, face burning.

It wasn't that she'd interrupted. Everyone's kid interrupts. It was that my whole team had just heard me plead with a two-year-old. And I'd heard it too.

That night at 11:40pm I was lying in bed typing "how to work from home with a toddler" and then "toddler interrupts every zoom call".

Everything it told me, I'd already tried:

🛏️ Book calls in nap time. She dropped her nap two months ago.

🧶 A busy bag. I'd packed one that morning, pompoms and pipe cleaners in a zip bag. They were across the whole floor in 4 minutes.

🍎 Snacks at the desk. One bowl bought me one slide.

📱 The iPad. It honestly works, right up until the call ends and the fight to take it back starts. Some days that fight was longer than the call.

Every fix got me to the start of a call. None of them got me through one.

On Saturday morning I finally opened a message I'd been avoiding. Dana from my team, who has three kids, had written to me privately ten minutes after the meeting.

"Please don't feel bad about today. Mine did exactly that for years. Can I tell you what I worked out?"

She said her kids never came for the meeting. They came for her going still. On a call she sits down, goes quiet, stares at a screen, and stops doing anything a small person can see. She stops being interesting. And that's exactly when their hands run out of things to do.

I read it three times.

Because it was true. My daughter could play for ages while I unloaded the dishwasher. It was only ever when I sat down and went silent. The interruptions weren't following the call. They were following the stillness.

Dana had one rule. Before the laptop opens, something goes on the floor at her feet that has a lot of steps and makes no noise.

I had never once thought about the noise.

Hers was a soft felt busy board. Buckles, zips, laces, snaps, little velcro pieces. None of it makes a sound on a call.

I thought it looked a bit babyish. I ordered one anyway, because another closure day was on the calendar.

She had a cough the Tuesday it arrived, so she was home. At 9:55 I unzipped it under the desk and handed her the page with the buckles. Then I opened the laptop.

It was a 40 minute call. She came up once, to show me a buckle she'd done up by herself, then sat back down between my feet and started on the laces. I muted once. The cough was mine.

Now the board comes out when the laptop opens. She sees me sit down and goes to find it.

The TV still goes on some afternoons and I don't feel bad about it. This is just one more thing, and it's the one I reach for first on call days.

I gave that presentation two weeks later from the same kitchen table. She was underneath it doing the same buckle over and over, and I got to the last slide.

If she always seems to find you the second you go quiet, it isn't the call and it isn't you. You went still, and her hands ran out of things.

Even if you don't get this one, try putting something silent with lots of steps at your feet before your next call starts. Before, not during.

200 words. That's the average for a 2-year-old. My son had 6.

I had been telling myself he was fine for months.

The kind of "fine" where I kept adding one more thing to our bedtime routine, praying something would click.

Reading a little longer at bedtime. Adding another Ms. Rachel song to the car ride. Buying another set of flashcards.

Convincing myself each new thing would be the one that clicked.

Nothing clicked.

Then we went to my niece's 2nd birthday party. That was the day it hit me.

She's 4 months younger than my son. 

She spent the whole party running up to her mom saying "cake please", "more juice", "look mama look." 

Full little sentences.

Meanwhile my son sat on my lap the whole time, pointing at things and grunting.

When we were leaving, my niece followed us to the driveway to wave goodbye. She said "bye Auntie" clear as day.

My son was on my hip. Silent.

The next Monday I called our pediatrician's office and asked for the first available appointment. 

They squeezed us in on Thursday.
 
The appointment lasted 12 minutes total. 

She measured him. Weighed him. Listened to his heart. Then asked if I had any concerns.
 
I told her he only had 6 words. That he understood everything I said but wouldn't speak. That every kid I knew his age was stringing sentences together and mine was still pointing.
 
She looked at his chart for maybe 4 seconds and said "he's within range for boys. Some are just late talkers. Come back at 2.5 if you're still worried."
 
I sat in the parking lot afterward for 20 minutes trying to figure out why I felt worse than when I walked in.
 
Because I knew. I already knew.
 
The signs had been there for months and I'd been finding a reason to ignore every one of them.
 
He stopped babbling around 14 months. I told myself he was just quiet.
 
He'd grunt and point instead of trying to say what he wanted. I told myself he was just efficient.
 
He shut down every time I asked him to say a word. I told myself he was just stubborn.
 
At his 18-month checkup he had 3 words. I told myself the pediatrician said boys just talk later.
 
At his 2-year checkup he had 6. I told myself at least it was more than 3.
 
Every red flag, I painted white.
 
That night I couldn't sleep. I sat on the couch with my phone and started Googling.
 
Somewhere around midnight I found a comment that stopped me cold.
 
"Between 20 and 30 percent of late talkers never fully catch up on their own. And the first 36 months of a kid's life is when the brain is wiring itself for language. After age 3, the wiring slows down."
 
My son had 12 months left in that window.
 
I sat there and stared at the wall for probably 20 minutes.
 
Because everything I'd been doing suddenly made sense in a way I didn't want it to.
 
I'd read to him every single night since he was born. Narrated my entire day out loud like a lunatic. Cut screens. Did Ms. Rachel songs in the car. Signed up for early intervention. 

Bought $200 worth of flashcards from Lovevery. Subscribed to Speech Blubs. Put him in daycare so he'd be around other kids.
 
None of it had worked.
 
And I finally understood why.
 
Kids don't build speech by hearing words. They build it by actually trying to say them.
 
Every single thing I'd been doing — my son was on the receiving end. He was passive. 

He was listening but he was never DOING.
 
It's the difference between watching someone ride a bike and being put on one. You can watch a bike your whole life and never learn to ride it.
 
Speech pathologists call it cause-and-effect play. It's the #1 technique they use in-clinic. 

And it works because the kid is the one driving it — pressing, hearing, and trying to repeat, hundreds of times a day, without any pressure or adult hovering.
 
I sat there at 1am and realized I'd been trying to teach my son to talk by talking AT him for 2 years.
 
The next morning I called the pediatrician back and asked for a formal speech therapy referral. 

The waitlist for a private speech pathologist near me was 6 months.
 
I couldn't wait 6 months.

So I started doing my own research. 

I joined 4 different Facebook groups for late talker parents. I followed every speech pathologist I could find on Instagram. I read Reddit threads until 1am looking for what actually worked for kids like mine.
 
Two days in, I saw a post that stopped me.

A mom whose son had been in the exact same spot as mine — understanding everything but not speaking — had found something that worked. 

It was a sound book — designed by speech pathologists.

She said her son got obsessed with it right away. 

Every page had pictures he could press to hear the word out loud. There was also a game mode where the book would say a word, and he had to find the picture that matched.

He'd sit with it for 30 minutes at a time saying the words along with the book. 

It was practice for him, but without any pressure.
 
And once the words felt easier to say, he started using them everywhere.

It sounded almost too good. And that was the problem.
 
Because I'd been down this road before. 

I'd already spent $180 on Lovevery flashcards that my son ignored after a week.
 
Two months of Speech Blubs at $12/month that he barely touched. 

A stack of Melissa & Doug learning toys collecting dust in his closet.

Nothing had worked.

And I know every kid is different, so what worked for her son might not work for mine.

But it was $50. And I was desperate. So I ordered it.
 
The first week I didn't see much. He held it, pressed some buttons, wandered off. I remember thinking great, another $50 down the drain.
 
But by week two, he'd started sitting with it every morning after breakfast. On his own. I didn't put it in front of him. 

He'd get up, pull it off the shelf, and sit on the rug flipping pages.
 
The game mode was what really got him. The book would call out "find the elephant" and he'd have to press the elephant. He was thrilled every time he got it right. He'd play it over and over.
 
By week three I heard him. He was mumbling the words back to the book while he played. Not to me. To the book. But he was saying them.
 
By week four he was making sounds along with the book. Not real words yet. But attempts. Effort.
 
Something was happening.
 
About a month in, I was making dinner and he walked up to me at the counter and said "up." With his arms out.
 
He wanted to be picked up.
 
He'd never once asked me for anything with a word. He'd always grab my leg and whine. 

I put down the spatula, picked him up, and cried into his hair.
 
Because in 2 years, that had never happened.
 
Not once.
 
Two weeks later he said his cousin's name for the first time. 

Three weeks after that he asked for milk instead of screaming at the fridge.
 
After that he wouldn't stop. He was trying new words every single day. Some clear, some garbled, some just attempts. But he was doing it. He was talking.
 
Last week I took him to the grocery store. He pointed at the fish tank and said "fish." 

A stranger overheard him and smiled at me.
 
First time in 2 years I didn't feel embarrassed at the store.
 
We went back for his 2.5 year checkup last month.
 
Same pediatrician. Same office.
 
He'd gone from 6 words to over 50.
 
She looked at his chart from 6 months ago and then looked at me. She said "I don't even know what to write here."

She told me I could go ahead and cancel the speech therapy referral — he wouldn't need it anymore.
 
She wrote down the name of the sound book and nodded.
 
And here's the part I didn't expect.
 
I got myself back too.
 
I stopped Googling "how many words should a 2-year-old have" at 2am every night. 

I stopped avoiding the family group chat. I stopped dreading playdates. 

I stopped watching every other kid's mouth at the park to see how many words they had that mine didn't.
 
I got to just be his mom again. Not his monitor.
 
The book was designed by speech pathologists. It has 500 clearly spoken words in it.
 
Every page has a red start button and icons he could press to hear each word.
 
There were themed pages for the zoo, the doctor's office, construction, the solar system, feelings, opposites — 23 themed worlds in total.
 
And each page had its own little game he'd play over and over.
 
My son had free access to any of them, whenever he wanted, just by pressing a button.
 
Which is the part I didn’t realize was so important.
 
He was in control. He decided when to press it, which word to hear, and how many times to hear it.
 
That's when learning actually sticks. When the kid is the one driving it.
 
There's also a phonics mode where the book teaches him each letter's sound. 

So beyond learning words, he was starting to piece together how they were built.
 
It's screen-free, and USB-C rechargeable so we're not fighting over dead batteries.
 
And it's safety tested for little hands.
 
The pages are thick and tear-proof so he can't rip them no matter how rough he plays with it.
 
And unlike an iPad, when he's done with it he's calm. Not amped up. Not melting down.
 
It's the only thing that finally worked.
 
I'm not saying it's a miracle. I'm not saying it will work for every kid overnight.
 
But I am saying if your kid is where mine was — understanding everything and just not able to get the words out — this is worth trying while there's still time in the window that matters.

bodyText:
I watched her do this from the couch and didn't say a word, because I couldn't get up.

This is our hallway.
Knee height, purple crayon, big loops.
The crayon's still on the floor where she snapped it.
I could see her the whole time from where I was feeding the baby.
She did it slowly.
She kept checking if I was watching.
I was. I just couldn't do anything about it.
The baby carrier hanging above it is the part that gets me.
Everything in this photo is about the baby, except her mark.
I'll explain.

When Max was born, Evie was two and a half.

He feeds about eight times a day, 40 minutes each. For the first two weeks she kissed his head every morning like he was a present someone had left for her.

Then she worked out what a feed means.

It means mommy sits down and can't get up.

So every feed, she found something. She climbed the back of the couch. She opened the fridge and stood in it. She drew on the hallway wall, low down, right where I could see it and couldn't reach it. She pulled every tissue out of the box, one at a time, looking at me the whole way.

Eight times a day. I started to dread the little snuffling noises Max makes when he's hungry, because I knew what came next.

Everyone said she's jealous, it's normal, you ride it out. So I rode it out, and tried everything else too:

🧺 The special feeding-time basket, with books and toys that only came out for feeds. Tipped onto the rug in about three minutes, and she was back on the couch arm.

👶 "Involve her." She fetched me a nappy once, so proud of herself, and that job lasted one minute. That left 39 minutes of the feed.

🍎 A snack at every feed. She ate it. Then she wouldn't touch her dinner.

📺 The TV at every feed. It worked, I won't pretend it didn't. But eight feeds a day is a lot of TV, and I could feel it adding up in both of us.

Then one afternoon in week four, I was pinned in the corner of the couch halfway through a feed, and it went quiet. I leaned over as far as I could without unlatching him. The nappy cream. The whole tube, smeared into the cushions in big white handprints.

I didn't yell. I just cried. Sat there with the baby still feeding and cried where she could see me.

And she came over, climbed up next to me, put her face right up close to mine and said, "Mommy sad?"

That undid me. She wasn't trying to be bad. She was right there, worried about me, and I'd spent weeks thinking of her as the problem.

That night at 2:10am, feeding again, I typed "toddler acting out while I feed the baby" and then "toddler jealous of newborn". Every answer said extra attention, one-on-one time, be patient.

I was never alone with her. That was the whole problem.

At the six-week home visit, the child health nurse sat on our ottoman with her notes while I fed Max. Evie did her whole routine. Up the couch. Down. Tissue box. Fridge door.

The nurse watched the entire feed and didn't write a thing. Then she said, "She's not jealous of the baby. She's jealous of your hands."

I laughed. Then I couldn't stop thinking about it.

For 40 minutes, my hands are full and hers are empty. Every other part of the day I'm her climbing frame, her helper, her toy. The feed is the one time I can't be. So her hands go looking for something, and what's in reach is the fridge and the wall.

Nothing I'd tried lasted as long as a feed.

She needed a job that was only hers, right next to me, with enough steps to outlast her brother.

I figured that works on other people's kids. I ordered a pink felt busy board anyway. A soft one that zips shut like a book, with buckles, zips, laces and snaps across the pages.

One rule. It comes out when the feeding pillow comes out, and goes away when the pillow does. It's not an anytime toy. It's her feed job.

The first feed, she did the buckle page, then undid every lace, then asked me to do them back up so she could undo them again. Max finished. I looked at the clock. She hadn't left the couch once.

That was three weeks ago.

Now when Max makes his hungry noises, Evie says "baby's hungry" and goes to get her board. She sits against my arm and works through the pages while he feeds. Sometimes she tells him about it. "Max. Buckle. Click."

I get to look at both of them. I drink my water while it's still cold. Some feeds I actually close my eyes.

The TV still goes on some afternoons when I'm wrecked. It's just not eight times a day anymore, and I'm not crying on the couch.

If you're feeding a newborn while your toddler climbs the walls: she isn't being naughty, and you're not doing it wrong. Her hands just have nothing to do at the one time yours can't help.

I've written it all out because a few moms asked. 👇 The exact board is linked below if you want a look.

Even if you skip this one, try giving her one job tomorrow that only comes out at feed time. It might get you through a whole feed. 🤍
